zones.name: Launching to orbit from an unflagged platform on the high seas
zones.essay:
The idea is to build a floating platform on the high seas, the open ocean beyond any country's coastal zones, fly no country's flag on it, fire a rocket into orbit from it, and leave whatever reaches orbit off every country's register. It joins the law of the sea, which governs the platform, space law, which governs the rocket and its cargo, and national licensing and export laws, which govern the people and the parts. The appeal is that the space treaties name a launching country partly by its territory or facility, and a platform with no flag seems to be neither.

The settled part comes first. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, usually called UNCLOS, says the high seas are open to all countries (Article 87). Its list of freedoms includes sailing, flying over and building installations "permitted under international law", and the list is not closed, although it does not mention rockets. Launching from the sea is an old practice. The US Navy fired a V-2 from the carrier USS Midway in 1947, and the company Sea Launch placed satellites in orbit from a converted oil rig on the equatorial Pacific from 1999 to 2014. Also settled is that a ship with no nationality may be boarded on the high seas by a warship of any country so that its right to a flag can be checked (UNCLOS Article 110). The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main space treaty, makes each member answer for "national activities" in space, including those of private bodies, which need authorisation and continuing supervision (Article VI). It makes liable any member that launches or procures a launch, or from whose "territory or facility" an object is launched (Article VII). The Liability Convention and the Registration Convention use the same words to define a "launching State".

Treaties bind countries and do not bind private people directly. Law reaches a person through national statutes. A US citizen, or a US company, needs a federal licence to launch "outside the United States" (51 USC 50904), and a foreign company controlled by US citizens can need one too. Britain's Outer Space Act 1986 applies to UK nationals and UK companies for launching, procuring a launch or any activity in outer space, and unlicensed activity is an offence under that Act. The space lawyer Armel Kerrest describes the treaty rule as placing every activity under the supervision of the state whose nationals conduct it.

Other points are open. The treaties do not define "facility". Nobody has decided whether a platform that no country has registered can be the facility of any country. Reading the text, it seems that a facility has to belong to a state to count, so an unflagged platform would satisfy neither the territory test nor the facility test. That leaves the first test, the state that "launches or procures", and the treaties do not say whether a country procures a launch merely because its citizens paid for it. Writers treated even the flagged version as hard. An article in the Journal of Legal Research says launching from the high seas, from a platform registered in a state outside the Liability Convention, by an international private consortium, made it hard to name the launching state. Alla Pozdnakova of the University of Oslo has said that some unauthorised projects may become possible because on the sea there is no real authority to supervise them, and that so far the US rule on its own citizens has kept this from being a problem. Whether Article 110 applies to a fixed structure, as opposed to a ship, is also an inference that no court has settled. None of this has been tested at orbital scale.

Whether the result would be unlawful needs care. Failing to register does not make the object an illegal thing under any treaty. The Registration Convention places the duty on launching countries. If no state qualifies, reading the text, no state has broken that duty, and if one does qualify, that state is the one in breach. The founders' exposure comes from national law, which depends on who they are.

Suppose a group tries it. The first contact with government comes through the parts. Rockets are treated as weapons technology by export regimes. Boeing, the manager of Sea Launch, paid a $10 million penalty in 1998 after US officials counted 207 violations of US export rules, and its export licences were suspended for about two months. US rules make it unlawful to export listed items without a licence, and they reach persons abroad under US jurisdiction who take custody of such items (22 CFR 127.1). A group would need rockets built entirely from uncontrolled parts or from a country willing to sell them, and any seller is then a procuring party with its own regulator. The second contact is the port. A rig or barge has to leave a harbour in some country, and that country's law applies while it is there. Insurance comes next. Licensing laws are where launch insurance is normally required, and the US figure runs up to $500 million, while the owners of the stationary residential ship MS Satoshi found in 2020 that no insurer would cover them at all. The third contact is radio. Tracking and flight-safety links need frequencies, which are coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), whose members are countries. The American company Swarm paid $900,000 in 2018 for unlicensed satellites launched from India. The fourth contact is a warship, since a platform with no flag gives any navy a stated ground for coming aboard if it counts as a ship.

If everything went right, the satellite would reach orbit with no entry on a register. It would gain little from that. Article II of the treaty still stops any country taking orbit as territory, and if the object caused damage, the injured country would pursue the builders in whatever courts could reach them.

The potential is small and real only at the low end. A crew made up entirely of nationals of a country with no space statute, using a rocket built without controlled parts, might break no licensing law at all, although the states of its suppliers and bankers may disagree. The strongest lawful version flies a real flag and holds a licence from a real state, as Sea Launch did, and that gives up the point of the exercise. The nearest real cases are Sea Launch, the Italian platform off Kenya, Swarm, and the Chinese barge launches of recent years, all of them done under a state.

odds.why: A group could perhaps build the hardware, but the parts, port, insurance and radio links each pass through a government first. Legal standing is close to none, since a platform with no flag can be boarded and an object on no register has no state to defend it. Money is scarce because insurers and banks need a responsible state. No one has tried this at orbital scale.

rules.says: The high seas are open to all countries, and they may build installations permitted under international law.
A warship may board a ship with no nationality on the high seas to check its right to a flag.
Countries answer for national space activities, including private ones, which need authorisation and continuing supervision.
A country that launches or procures a launch, or from whose territory or facility an object is launched, is liable for damage.
A launching state, defined in the same words, must enter the object on a registry and tell the UN.
A US citizen or US company needs a licence to launch outside the United States.
UK nationals and companies need a licence for launching, procuring a launch or any activity in outer space.

zones.name: Launch ship under a flag of convenience
zones.essay:
This is the lawful relative of launching from an unflagged platform. A company registers its launch platform and support ship in a country that offers light rules, sails to a spot on the open ocean, and launches satellites there under a licence from some other country. It combines a ship's flag, the freedom of the high seas and the rules on orbit. It has been done many times, so the interest lies in how much it really changes.

A flag of convenience is a shipping practice. Every ship has one country's nationality, and the owner may choose a country with low fees and light supervision that the ship may never visit. UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, requires a genuine link between the ship and the flag state and requires the flag state to supervise it (Articles 91 and 94). Sea Launch used this pattern. It was founded in 1995 by four companies from Norway, Russia, Ukraine and the United States, was registered in the Cayman Islands, and put its rig Odyssey and its ship Sea Launch Commander on Liberia's register. Liberia is party to none of the four main space treaties, according to the UN's status table of 1 January 2026. The rockets were Zenit-3SL, assembled in Long Beach, California. By 2014 the company had launched thirty-two successfully, with three failures and one partial failure, before it stopped after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The settled parts are these. The law on board the ship is Liberian, in the same way that the law on any ship is its flag state's. That governs matters such as crew and safety. Space law then applies separately. The Outer Space Treaty makes a country answer for national activities in space (Article VI) and makes liable any country that launches or procures a launch, or from whose territory or facility an object is launched (Article VII). US citizens and companies need a licence for launching abroad under 51 USC 50904. Boeing, as a US company managing the venture, fell under US export rules wherever the rig sailed, and in 1998 it agreed to pay $10 million after the State Department listed 207 violations. Its licences had been suspended on 27 July and were then restored. US Customs also tried to stop the Zenit rockets, classed as missiles, entering California without a munitions import licence, and that was settled in the company's favour. The International Transport Workers' Federation criticised the Liberian registration in 1997, and the company reached an agreement with it in May 1999 allowing union inspectors.

What remains open is who the launching state was and is in such a case. The Liability Convention calls the state whose "territory or facility" is used a launching state and a participant in a joint launch. Whether a flag makes a rig the flag state's facility is unanswered, because the treaty does not define the word, and if the flag state is not a party, the treaty has no hold on it at all. An article in the Journal of Legal Research says these features, a high-seas launch from a platform registered in a non-party, by a private consortium with no agreement among the states concerned, made it hard to say who was liable, and that the question went to the UN's space committee. The result was General Assembly resolution 59/115 in 2004, which states that nothing in it is an authoritative reading of the treaties. It recommends national laws and agreements between states on joint launches. So the gap was discussed and left in place. Reading the text, it seems that a flag state outside the treaties owes treaty victims nothing, while the states of the licensees and of the customers who procure the launch remain liable, and a victim could choose among them, since Kerrest explains that launching states are liable jointly and severally. No claim of this kind has been brought.

The flag of convenience also fails to deliver what founders want. Suppose a group takes this route to launch its own station. The flag state's law applies on the ship and does not follow the rocket. The station in orbit falls under whichever launching state registers it, with legal control over everyone aboard under Article VIII of the treaty. The group's choice of Liberia has no bearing on that. Its nationals remain under their home licensing laws, and its parts remain under export rules. Pacific island countries raised concerns at the UN in 1999 about oil slicks from unused fuel in discarded boosters, so neighbours also have a voice. Sea Launch itself went bankrupt in 2009 and came out of it under majority Russian ownership in 2010. Its assets were later bought by S7 Group and the ships moved to Russia, which shows that a rig can pass from a multinational venture to owners in one country.

The real potential is commercial. A platform can reach the equator, where the Earth's spin gives a rocket extra speed, and avoid dealing with a host country. Gerasimos Rodotheatos, who researches sea launches, points out that many equatorial countries are hard to work with, and a vessel lets an operator choose its location. China has launched more than a dozen missions from ocean platforms since 2019, and Italy has said it will reopen its platform off Kenya. For a founder, the strongest version is a licensed launch company that owns its own launch ship and sells access to a settlement, so that one step of the supply route stays under its own management. That gives income and some bargaining power, and no independence.

odds.why: Sea Launch did this 36 times, so a repeat by a well-funded company is plausible. The legal position is workable because a real flag state and a real licensing state stand behind it. Holding is fair since nobody needs to board a properly flagged ship, though export rules halted Sea Launch's licences for two months in 1998. It gives no independence, so recognition is close to nil.

zones.name: Launching to orbit from an aircraft over the open ocean
zones.essay:
An aircraft carries a rocket under its wing, flies out over open ocean, and drops it. The rocket lights and goes to orbit. This route combines two different zones, the air over the high seas, where every country is free to fly and none holds authority, and low Earth orbit. It is worth attention because at the moment of release the launch site is a moving aircraft, and no country's soil or water lies beneath it.

The working example is Pegasus, a small rocket built by Orbital Sciences and first flown on 5 April 1990 from a NASA B-52. Later flights used a converted airliner, a Lockheed L-1011 called Stargazer. The aircraft released the rocket at about 12,000 metres over open ocean. It took off from places including California, Florida, Virginia, the Kwajalein range in the Pacific and the Canary Islands in the Atlantic. So a US-owned aircraft could leave Spanish soil, release a US rocket over the sea, and reach orbit.

The settled law gives each piece a home. UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, says every country is free to fly over the high seas (Article 87). The Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, says an aircraft has the nationality of the country that registered it and can be on one register only (Articles 17 and 18). The same treaty says that the rules over the high seas are those set under the Convention (Article 12). Under the Tokyo Convention of 1963, the country of registration has power over offences on board in flight. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, makes liable any country that launches or procures a launch, or from whose "territory or facility" an object is launched (Article VII). Licensing laws reach the people. A US citizen or company needs a licence to launch outside the United States (51 USC 50904).

The open point is the same word as for a sea platform. Nobody has ruled that a registered aircraft is the "facility" of the state that registered it, although reading the text, a carrier aircraft listed on a state's register seems a natural fit, and the state of registry has clear control over it. A further open question is the country from whose airport the flight departed. The rocket leaves that country's territory physically attached to the aircraft, and Spain, in the Canary Islands flights, is one example. Whether the airport state's territory counts as used for the launch is unanswered, because the Liability Convention does not address it. The UN's 2004 resolution on the launching state (59/115) recommends that countries make agreements on joint launches, and it leaves the wording unchanged. These questions have not come up in practice, because the flights ran under government licences and no damage claim is known.

Consider a founder who tries to remove the state from this picture. An unregistered aircraft has no right to enter any country's airspace, because Article 5 of the Chicago Convention gives flight rights to the aircraft of countries that have joined. So the carrier needs a register, or it has to take off from a country that agrees to let it fly with no nationality, and that country has then allowed the use of its soil. Rockets are also treated as defence items by export rules. US rules make it unlawful to export listed defence articles and services without a licence (22 CFR 127.1), and the aircraft's own maintenance, crew licences and fuel come through regulators. Radio links for flight safety and tracking need frequencies coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union, whose members are countries. When the rocket drops, any navy or air force in the region will want to know what it is, and air defence identification zones (areas where a state, by its own declaration, asks aircraft to identify themselves) extend past national airspace near many coasts.

Reading the text, it seems that the aircraft route is stronger than the sea route on one narrow point. UNCLOS lets a warship board a ship with no nationality, and an aircraft in flight cannot be boarded. Article 110 extends the right of visit to military aircraft as visitors, and it speaks of ships as the target. Against that, an aircraft has to land within hours. Article 3 bis of the Chicago Convention limits the use of weapons against civil aircraft, and whether that protects an aircraft with no state behind it is untested. So the aircraft gains nothing lasting.

The potential is real for ordinary commercial launch. An operator gets flexibility in where it launches and what orbit it reaches, and avoids a fixed coastal launch pad. For a project seeking distance from states, the strongest version is a licensed company owning a carrier aircraft registered in a state with few rules, launching for a settlement it also supplies. The object would still go onto a launching state's register. Everything then rests on that state, as with any other launch.

odds.why: Pegasus shows the method works, and a private group with money could fly one under licence. The legal position is reasonable only while an aircraft stays on a state's register. Aircraft have to land often, and that gives governments regular contact. No state would see it as anything other than a launch service.

zones.name: An unrecognised state acting as a launching state
zones.essay:
An unrecognised state is a place with a real government and population whose statehood few or no countries accept, such as Somaliland or Northern Cyprus. A project might ask one of these governments to act as its launching state. The unrecognised state would authorise the launch, keep a register and take responsibility, so that the project would sit under a friendly authority that holds real land. It combines the zone of unrecognised states with orbit.

It helps to see the formal position first. The space treaties are open to "States". The UN's table of treaty members, as of 1 January 2026, has no row for Taiwan, Somaliland, Northern Cyprus or Abkhazia. Taiwan shows that the absence is more about politics than ability. It has its own government and elections, and the UN since 1971 has treated the People's Republic of China as the holder of China's seat. North Korea shows the reverse. It is a UN member, heavily isolated, and it has joined all four main space treaties, and the UN lists an object on its register. So the ability to use the system depends on recognition by other states and the UN.

Under the Registration Convention, only a launching state, or a qualifying intergovernmental organisation, can register an object and report it to the UN Secretary-General. A self-declared state that tried to report would need the Secretary-General's office to accept it as a state, and the treaty gives it no way to insist. To be a member of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), which coordinates frequencies, a country outside the UN needs the agreement of two-thirds of members. That sets a very high bar.

The law also gives such places some standing. Statehood, under Article 3 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, is said not to depend on recognition, and it lists four tests. Reading that together with Article VII of the Outer Space Treaty, it seems that a place meeting those tests, with a rocket leaving its soil, might be said to be a launching state in fact. If it has not joined, the treaty text does not reach it, and the parent state may be treated as the responsible party in law. The parent state's position is what other countries usually adopt. Somalia, for instance, has signed the Outer Space Treaty, and Somaliland's soil is treated by most countries as Somalia's. Reading the text, a launch from Somaliland might make Somalia a launching state under the wording "territory", even though Somalia has no control there. The English Court of Appeal's 2010 decision on flights to Northern Cyprus points the same way in air law. KTHY, which the court described as a Turkish airline, asked Britain for permission to fly to Ercan airport in the north. The court held that the Chicago Convention gave the Republic of Cyprus sovereignty over the whole island, even where it lacks control, and that the UK would breach the treaty if it granted the permit. No court has applied this reasoning to a space launch, so the parallel is an inference.

What is open is what would happen in practice. No unrecognised state has launched to orbit. Other countries might hold the parent state responsible, might hold the unrecognised government responsible under general rules, or might do neither and look to the nationals and suppliers. Nothing settles how an injured country would bring a claim against a government it does not recognise.

Follow it through. Parts come first. US export rules apply to listed items wherever they go (22 CFR 127.1), and sanctions may apply to the host. Then the host would have to accept exposure to damage claims. The rocket would pass over or near other countries' airspace. Frequencies would have to be filed through some ITU member, and a sponsor willing to do so would be accepting a share of the responsibility. Banks and insurers look for a recognised regulator, and an unrecognised government has none to show them. A sponsor state might register the launch instead, as Turkey in principle could for Northern Cyprus. That removes the question of status, because the sponsor is then the launching state, and it also moves control to the sponsor.

The attraction to the host is prestige, and a launch could serve as evidence of real government. A launch site does not give recognition, however, since recognition is a political decision made government by government. Somaliland, for example, has won limited ties through other means, including its 2020 cooperation agreement with Taiwan.

The potential is limited. The strongest version is a recognised sponsor state with a launch site on the unrecognised state's soil and a treaty between the two, with launches under the sponsor's flag. That gives the host some income and status, and it leaves the question of statehood where it was.

odds.why: No unrecognised state has launched to orbit, and it would need a sponsor or a large investment. The UN system has no place for it without recognition. A launch might add some evidence of real government, which gives it a slightly higher chance of recognition than other space routes, though recognition turns on politics. Neighbours and export controls can stop it long before that.

zones.name: A digital nation with a satellite as its territory
zones.essay:
Online nations have citizens, websites and sometimes constitutions, and they have no land. A satellite looks like a way to fix that. The idea is to put a small object in orbit, declare it to be the nation's territory, and point to it when anyone says the nation has no place of its own. This joins digital countries and low Earth orbit, and it has already been done once.

Asgardia is the case. A Russian engineer named Igor Ashurbeyli announced it in Paris on 12 October 2016, and people joined online, over 100,000 within two days. On 12 November 2017 a Cygnus cargo craft, launched on an Antares rocket from Virginia, released the 2.8 kilogram satellite Asgardia-1. Asgardia then described itself as the first nation with all its territory in space. The satellite burned up on 12 September 2022 and no replacement has been reported. A press release of 2025 claims over one million citizens, and no state or UN body recognises it.

The settled law on this is clear. The Montevideo Convention of 1933 sets the usual tests for statehood, and one of them is a defined territory. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 says that outer space cannot be appropriated by any country by claim, use, occupation or other means (Article II). Legal scholars argued that because US companies launched Asgardia's satellite on a NASA-funded mission, the United States was the launching state and remained responsible, and that Article VIII of the treaty kept authority over the object with the state of registry. A satellite in law is an object. It is property under some country's law, and it is no more territory than a car is.

Some points are more open than that makes them sound. Asgardia's backers reasoned that by becoming a nation they could escape the restrictions on private space activity. No rule says only existing states may become states. The ban in Article II is written to stop states and, in the widely held view, those acting through them from acquiring space, and it has not been tested against a brand new entity that claims only its own objects. Reading the text, it seems that claiming an object differs from claiming a part of space, so the Article II ban may not be the decisive obstacle. The territory test is. Whether a manufactured object can ever count as territory under Montevideo is untested. It seems unlikely, since ships and aircraft, which have the nationality of a state, are not treated as that state's territory for most purposes, and no ship is known to have gained statehood for anyone.

Here is what happens when someone tries. A digital nation buys a ride to orbit through a licensed launch broker. The launch provider's country is a launching state and handles the licensing and safety review. The US, for instance, requires a licence for launches within it (51 USC 50904) and would review the payload. The radio link needs a licence through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. The American company Swarm was fined $900,000 for putting satellites up without a licence, so the broker will insist on one. That places the object on a state's books, usually through the operator's home country, and Article VIII does the rest. The nation's members remain citizens of their home countries, pay their home taxes, and carry their home passports. A passport with no state behind it has no code in border systems. A digital currency faces ordinary financial rules. So the satellite changes nothing about how any of them live.

The lifetime of the object is another limit. A small satellite in low orbit falls back to Earth within a few years, as Asgardia-1 did in under five. A nation whose territory has burned up must buy another, and its claim would then be interrupted. The operator could raise the orbit, but the cost then grows with the size.

What such a project does gain is publicity and something real to show to members. It can run experiments, run elections and raise money. Asgardia's parliament has met in Vienna, and it held a congress in Dubai in 2025. Satellites can also carry stored data and run servers. Cloud Constellation's SpaceBelt plan of 2015 to 2018 offered orbital storage as a way past national data laws, and trade reporters pointed out that data rules like Europe's follow the people whose data it is. It needed $480 million and raised far less.

The strongest version is honest about what it is, a voluntary association registered as a company or nonprofit in an ordinary country, using a satellite as a symbol and a platform. That is lawful and cheap by space standards. It has a low chance of any government treating it as more.

odds.why: Asgardia has already done this, so a repeat is simple. The satellite stays under the launching and registering state, and that keeps its legal value low. Money comes only from members and sponsors. No government has to act against a satellite this small, and none has recognised one.

No country can take over outer space by claim, use, occupation or other means.
The state of registry keeps control of the object.
A launch in the United States or by a US citizen abroad needs a licence.

zones.name: Buying a station already in orbit
zones.essay:
Instead of launching a new station, a group might buy one that is already in orbit from a government or company, in the way someone might buy an old oil platform at sea. The buyer would then seek to run it as a place of its own. This combines buying from a state, low Earth orbit and the abandoned-platform idea. Satellites do change hands in orbit, so the mechanics are known, and a sale does not deliver what founders want.

Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, says that the state on whose registry an object is carried keeps jurisdiction and control over it and over its personnel, and that ownership is not affected by presence in space. The registry state therefore stays in charge after a sale, unless some other state takes over. Ownership and jurisdiction are separate things. A sale moves ownership, which is a question of private law. The Registration Convention gives no procedure for moving a registration to another state. Article II of that Convention says only that where there are several launching states, they decide among themselves which will register. A state that was not a launching state does not fit the definition. So a transfer to a non-launching state has no clear basis in the treaty text.

The UN has responded to this gap with recommendations. General Assembly resolution 59/115 of 2004 invited countries to share their practices on on-orbit transfer of ownership. Resolution 62/101 of 2007 recommends that after a change of supervision the state of registry, working with the appropriate state under Article VI, give the UN the date of the change, the new owner or operator, and any new orbit or function. It adds that if there is no state of registry, the appropriate state under Article VI could give that information. Resolutions like these recommend and do not bind. UN officials reported in 2016 that more states had been supplying such notices.

Real sales show the pattern. In 1984 the Space Shuttle Discovery recovered two broken satellites, Palapa B2 and Westar 6, and brought them back to Earth. Westar 6 was later sold to the Hong Kong company AsiaSat. That was a sale of hardware recovered on the ground. MirCorp is the nearest case for a habitat. In 2000 the Amsterdam-based company, with the Russian company RSC Energia as a major shareholder, got rights to run the Russian station Mir commercially for the rest of its life, and it paid for one crew's flight. The station stayed Russian. Russia brought it down in March 2001, the US export approval for a tether arrived too late, and MirCorp's money ran out. Article VIII never moved at all.

What remains open is how far a buyer can shift the Article VI duty to a state of its choice, and what happens when the launching state and the new supervising state disagree. Launching states remain liable for damage. Being a launching state is a historical fact about the launch, so a sale cannot end it, although states can agree among themselves who bears the cost, as Armel Kerrest explains. Reading the Liability Convention, the seller's state cannot escape liability merely by selling. That gives the seller's state a lasting reason to keep control or to refuse the sale. Whether a state could abandon an object outright is not addressed in the treaties. The space lawyer Michael Listner has discussed a signed waiver as a possible method, and it has not been tested.

Walk through a sale. Suppose a government decides to retire a station and a group offers to buy it. The seller's government has a right to refuse any buyer. If the station includes US parts, US export rules come into it, as MirCorp's tether showed, and Listner notes that moving a derelict satellite can raise the same rules. Operating the station requires radio frequencies that belong to a member state's filing at the International Telecommunication Union. Insurers will ask which state supervises the station. The supply flights come from a licensed launch provider. And the station has to be maintained, since a station that is not boosted falls. NASA's Inspector General has put the International Space Station's running cost at about $3 billion a year, and a group that buys a smaller station still has to pay to keep it up. If the station begins to fail, governments will want it brought down safely, since uncontrolled re-entry of something so large could cause damage on the ground. A launching state has a strong interest in insisting on that.

The buyer would have a station. It would live under the law of the registry state, or under a new state's law if all the governments involved agreed. A small friendly state as new supervising state might get the group light rules, with the same limits as any small-flag approach. The International Space Station partners, by contrast, each keep legal control over the modules they register (Article 5 of their 1998 agreement), which makes a sale of parts of it even harder.

So the potential is mainly practical. It might cost less than building new, and it brings real habitable space. The strongest version is a purchase with a seller's state remaining as supervisor, under a long contract with wide operating freedom. That delivers something like MirCorp, with more money and better luck, and it delivers no sovereignty.

odds.why: Satellites are sold in orbit, but a working crewed station has never been sold to a private owner. MirCorp only leased rights. The state of registry keeps control after a sale, so legal standing depends on friendly governments. Running costs are high and a seller can refuse.

zones.name: A settlement built on a contract like Starlink's Mars clause
zones.essay:
In October 2020 SpaceX put an unusual sentence in the terms of service for an early test of its Starlink internet service. Terms of service are a contract between a company and its customers. The clause said that for services on Mars, or in transit there by Starship or other colonization spacecraft, "the parties recognize Mars as a free planet and that no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities", with disputes settled by self-governing principles agreed at the time of settlement. The idea is to build the law of a settlement out of private contract, signed before departure. It combines the settlement of Mars with the kind of contract-based community found in digital nations.

Some of this is settled. A contract binds those who sign it. A customer and a company can agree on how to settle disputes between them, including choosing a set of rules. Courts on Earth routinely enforce choice-of-law and arbitration clauses within limits, although the limits depend on each country. No contract can release a government from a treaty, and no contract can take away powers that neither party holds. Under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, the United States bears responsibility for national activities in space, including those of its companies, which need authorisation and continuing supervision. An article in Völkerrechtsblog points out that the US Federal Communications Commission does much of this for SpaceX in practice. Article VIII gives the state of registry jurisdiction and control over its registered objects and personnel. So the US would not lose either power by reason of a private clause.

Whether the sentence is still in the terms is not known, and no court has ever ruled on it. No one has reached Mars under it. What the sentence means is itself open. It could be read as a mere statement of the parties' shared belief. It could be read as a choice of law, as an arbitration clause or as an agreement not to sue, each of which has a different effect. A law journal note at the University of Richmond said the clause tried to sidestep international law. The Völkerrechtsblog writer argues that it risks breach of Article II, since attempting to exclude other jurisdictions from Mars has the shape of a sovereign claim, and that its conduct would be attributed to the US. The same writer notes a further danger that runs the other way. In territorial disputes, courts have treated acts of administration by companies under national authority as establishing title for their state, so a private "free Mars" could one day be read by others as American colonisation. Reading the text, it seems that the clause is weak as a source of independence and could be useful as a private dispute-settlement rule between those who signed it. It is hard to say more without knowing what it would actually be used for.

Follow a settler. Before leaving, she signs a long agreement with the transport company. Its terms say that disputes go to an agreed process and that local rules apply on arrival. The launch is licensed, and the rocket is registered in the US or another launching state. On the way out, she is on a US-registered ship, under US control in the sense of Article VIII. She arrives at a base. A dispute breaks out over an injury. Under her contract, she takes it to a settlement panel, which rules against her. She then returns to Earth, or her family sues in California, where the original terms set California law for services on Earth. A court there would have to decide whether the Mars clause holds up, and courts may refuse to enforce a waiver of serious injury claims, and no contract waives criminal law. If a killing occurs, no contract can bar the home states of the victim and the suspect from acting, and the settlement cannot lawfully prevent the state of registry from exercising its control.

The contract also has limits from outside. It does not bind people who did not sign, such as a child born on Mars or a visitor from another country's base. A nonsignatory neighbour can ignore it. Article XII of the treaty lets representatives of other parties visit stations on a reciprocal basis, whatever a contract says. Bank accounts, shares and property on Earth are subject to ordinary national law, so a company that lost in court could be forced to pay there. Its FCC licences, launch licences and export permits give the US further practical leverage over the company itself.

A good deal of real order could still be built this way. Private communities on Earth, from cruise ships to gated towns to the ORBIS model lease studied by Alexander Salter, run largely on contract. Most disputes among neighbours would go to the settlement's own panel because that is cheap and close. The state of registry might simply choose not to intervene in small matters. In that situation, the contract would really govern everyday life for a long time, and it would not depend on anyone conceding sovereignty.

So the potential is in everyday order, and legal independence does not follow from it. The strongest version states plainly that it sits under the law of the state of registry, sets up an arbitration system whose awards can be enforced on Earth, and treats serious crime as the state's business. Treating Mars as free in a clause adds little to that, and it may bring the company unwanted scrutiny from regulators and from lawyers.

odds.why: Nobody has gone to Mars, and the clause itself has never been tested. Contracts can govern private disputes, but they bind no government and release no treaty duties. Hold is fair because of the distance, and the contract adds nothing to it. No state would recognise a settlement on this basis.

zones.name: Using space resource laws as a stepping stone
zones.essay:
Four countries have passed laws saying that a company may own what it extracts in space. A founder might try to build outward from that foothold. First comes a licence to mine, then ownership of what is mined, then a long-running base around the mine, then a claim that the people who live there have rights of their own. This combines space mining with the idea of a host state carving out a special zone. It is modelled on the way companies and mining camps have sometimes grown into governments on Earth.

The laws are real. The US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015 says a US citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid or space resource is entitled to whatever is obtained, including to possess, own, transport, use and sell it, in accordance with US international obligations (51 USC 51303). The Act also says that the United States does not by this law assert sovereignty or ownership over any celestial body. Luxembourg passed a similar law in 2017, followed by the United Arab Emirates and Japan. The Artemis Accords, non-binding principles with 78 signatories by 28 October 2026, say that extraction does not inherently constitute national appropriation under Article II of the Outer Space Treaty (Section 10). The treaty itself says bodies in space cannot be appropriated by claim, use, occupation or any other means. So the ground is off limits, and the extracted material is claimed as property under national law.

Opinion is divided on whether this is consistent. Luxembourg's own Council of State, which advises on new laws, said it was unclear whether international law allows this. Russia objected to the US executive order of April 2020 on space resources. The Moon Agreement of 1979, with 17 parties, treats the Moon's resources as the common heritage of humankind, to be managed under an international system yet to be written, and Saudi Arabia left that treaty with effect from January 2024. A For All Moonkind article suggests the exit may reflect a wish to follow countries building a new custom through domestic mining laws. Those who take the view that mining is allowed compare it to fishing on the high seas, where the fish become yours once you catch them and the sea does not. No court has ruled on the question. It remains open whether national grants of title bind other states, and whether they would be respected in a court outside the granting state.

The steps beyond ownership are less well supported. Owning what you mine gives no right to the place where you mine it. Reading the text, it seems that the US law's own disclaimer and Article II together stop the claim at the extracted material, and that a mining camp would be protected only by its licence and by Article VIII's rule that its objects stay the owner's. Exclusive mining rights in an area are also not granted by any of these laws. The Hague Space Resources Working Group adopted its Building Blocks for an international framework on 9 November 2019, and they are not a treaty. Long use could create expectations on the ground. It is hard to convert those into anything like territory. The Völkerrechtsblog writer notes that in territorial cases, conduct by companies under national authorisation has established title for their state, and this is exactly why a government licensing a mine would want to avoid that reading. Article II bars the same outcome directly.

Here is how a real project would play out. A company incorporates in the US or Luxembourg to get the resource law. It needs an authorisation, and Luxembourg treats it as a licence under supervision, much as for a bank or fund, so the choice of a friendly country is also a choice of regulator. US citizens need launch licences anyway under 51 USC 50904. The company lands equipment and begins taking ice. Its home state must supervise it (Article VI), and the state would be responsible for what it does. It would give notice of its activities, and under the Accords it can announce a safety zone. Workers then live on site under their employment contract and their home states' laws. A camp grows. Eventually some residents want a say over how the base runs, and a mining company then becomes something like a local government, as the East India Company or a company town did on Earth, though these took place under far weaker international rules on territory.

Money would be the first real barrier. Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries were both set up to mine asteroids, ran short of money, and were sold in 2018 and 2019. The customer is unclear, since water in space has value only if a market exists in space. If one forms, it may be other governments' programmes, and the camp would then rely on them.

Bank financing works best with secure title, so the legal doubt raises the cost. A company could reduce doubt by operating only under a large state's protection, and that again trades away independence.

The potential is real as a first step toward any lasting presence, because ownership of what is mined can fund a base, and the rules on it have moved in recent years in favour of operators. The trend in national laws has been toward private rights. The strongest version has a licensed mine under an Accords signatory, a large settled workforce, and a charter from the home state giving the camp its own local government. A later generation might use that history as a basis for self-rule under some new treaty. No rule provides a path from one to the other, and any such step would be a matter of politics for that later generation.

odds.why: Laws in four countries let companies own what they extract, so the first step exists, but no one has mined anything in space. Mining firms have run out of money. No law grants any right to the ground, so the later steps have no legal basis yet. A state would have to give up control willingly.

zones.name: A space elevator anchored on the high seas
zones.essay:
A space elevator would be a cable running from Earth's surface far into space, held taut by a counterweight at the top as the planet turns, with climbers carrying cargo along it. The scientist Bradley Edwards, working from 2000 with support from NASA's Institute for Advanced Concepts, suggested anchoring its base on a movable sea platform in the western equatorial Pacific, where lightning and hurricanes are less common. Such a platform on the high seas would need no host country. This combines an orbital megastructure with a place on the open ocean. It is worth study because it fits none of the existing legal categories neatly.

Each end has settled rules. UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, allows all countries to use the high seas, including building installations "permitted under international law" (Article 87). Ships have the nationality of one flag state (Article 92), and a ship without nationality can be boarded (Article 110). Any activity in space is a national activity for which a state answers, and which needs authorisation and continuing supervision (Outer Space Treaty, Article VI). Launching states are liable for damage (Article VII). The state of registry holds control over its registered objects (Article VIII). Space belongs to no one (Article II). The Chicago Convention gives countries sovereignty over air above their territory, while the air over the high seas is open to all (Article 1 of Chicago, Article 87 of UNCLOS). So a base on the equator over open ocean would have a cable crossing no national territory at the bottom.

The open questions are large and unanswered. Nobody knows what the structure is. Reading the text, a cable fixed to a platform on Earth might not be "launched into outer space" in the way a satellite is, although the seed cable that starts construction would have to be lifted from Earth, so that part looks like a launched object. If it counts as a space object, launching-state rules apply. The Registration Convention speaks of objects launched into Earth orbit or beyond, and the ribbon as a whole does not orbit in any ordinary sense. A climber would be neither an aircraft nor a launch vehicle in any clear way. The section passing through the air might also be an obstacle in the air, a matter for aviation safety rules under the Chicago Convention. Whether the sea base is a ship or an installation is also unanswered, because UNCLOS does not define "ship" and does not say plainly how it applies to a fixed structure over the deep sea. A mooring to the deep seabed raises a further question under the rules for the deep ocean floor. Nobody has ruled on any of this because the thing has never been built.

Physical facts weigh more than legal ones here. The material has never been made at the strength and length needed. Edwards's plan required a seed cable of 19,800 kilograms, then 207 climbers adding to it until the ribbon reached about 750 tons and could lift 20 tons per climber. If the ribbon broke, it could cause wide damage, and any launching state would be strictly liable for damage on Earth or to aircraft. The upper section would pass through the orbits of satellites of many states. Their owners would have a due regard claim under Article IX, and the movable platform is partly a way to shift the ribbon out of the path of tracked debris.

Now consider what would happen politically. Philip Ragan, co-author of a book on space elevators, said the first country to deploy one could have a 95 percent cost advantage and potentially control all space activities. That gives every major power a strong reason to care who runs it. Each could argue that the object threatens its satellites, and a warship has a right to board a ship with no nationality. A group that had a flag would have its flag state to protect it, and that state's control would then be the main issue. Its parts would be export-controlled. Its radio links would need ITU filings. Its financing, at this scale, would require governments.

The route has some potential in a distant future. A base on open ocean really could reduce one kind of political friction, because no coastal state has to host it. A flag state, or a consortium of states under a treaty, could own and run it, with something like the arrangements of the International Space Station. That would make it a place where many nationalities work and live, and the operator may hold real bargaining power, since everyone needs the route. The strongest version is a treaty-based international authority operating a flagged platform. It would not be a free country.

odds.why: No material strong enough exists, so this may never be built within 25 years. The law has no category for it, which keeps the legal odds uncertain. Its strategic value would draw major powers at once, and that makes holding hard. It would be run by states if built.

zones.name: Launching from a state outside the space treaties
zones.essay:
Four UN treaties form the core of space law, and not every country has joined them. A project might set up its launch site in a country that has not joined, expecting that the rules on licensing, liability and registration would then not apply to it. This combines a deal with a host state and a launch to orbit. It raises a basic question about what binds a country that never signed.

The numbers come first. As of 1 January 2026 the UN's status table shows 118 parties to the Outer Space Treaty, 100 to the Rescue Agreement, 100 to the Liability Convention and 77 to the Registration Convention. Many small countries have joined none of these, including Vanuatu, Nauru, Palau, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands. Liberia has joined none of the four. Somalia and Rwanda have signed the Outer Space Treaty without ratifying it, meaning they have not formally agreed to be bound. Iran is a useful example of a mixed record, with a signature only on the Outer Space Treaty and the Registration Convention and full membership of the Rescue Agreement and the Liability Convention. North Korea, by contrast, has joined all four, and the UN listed one object on its behalf by 2016.

Settled law on treaties is simple. A treaty binds those who join it. So a non-party has no treaty duty to register, and a party's duties do not pass to it. The Outer Space Treaty's rules on liability bind members only, and its text speaks of "State Party". It is also settled that a launch from a non-party's soil does not cancel the duties of any party involved. A company from a treaty country remains under its home state's supervision (Article VI), and if that state procures or launches, it is liable. A US citizen launching anywhere outside the United States needs a US licence (51 USC 50904). Britain's Outer Space Act applies to UK nationals and UK companies. The American company Swarm launched from India after being refused a licence and paid $900,000 anyway.

What is open is customary international law, the body of rules that bind countries because they generally follow them and treat them as law, whether or not a treaty says so. Ram Jakhu and Steven Freeland, in a 2016 paper, examined whether Articles I, II, VI and VII of the Outer Space Treaty reach states that never joined or have left. They accept that a treaty rule that has become custom can bind third states. An article in Völkerrechtsblog describes Articles II and III as customary, and it cites writers who go further and call the ban on national appropriation in Article II a peremptory rule, one no state can opt out of. Others are more cautious, and no court has ruled. The strongest candidate is the ban on claiming space, since the one serious claim, the 1976 Bogotá Declaration by eight equatorial countries over parts of geostationary orbit, did not win acceptance. The registration duty is the weakest. UN figures show non-parties and even parties leave objects off the list, and the UN office counts not being a party as one of the listed reasons for not registering. Reading the text and this practice together, it seems likely that liability for damage would be claimed against a non-party under general rules of state responsibility, although nobody can say how such a claim would go.

Follow a project through. A group signs with a small non-party government, which grants land and passes a decree authorising launches. That government now has the same problem any launching state has. If a stage falls on a neighbour, the neighbour will hold the host responsible whatever the treaties say. So the host will want insurance and a say in safety. The rocket's parts have to come from somewhere, and US rules make it unlawful to export listed defence items without a licence (22 CFR 127.1). Radio frequencies come through the International Telecommunication Union, which the host can use if it is a member, and a filing for satellites can then be made in its name. Banks and insurers will look at sanctions and export risk. Other governments may press the host directly. The result depends on how much pressure the host can absorb.

The nearest real case is OTRAG, a West German company based in Stuttgart, which from the 1970s tried to build cheap modular rockets. It tested them at Shaba North in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and at Seba Oasis in Libya, reaching heights of 20 to 50 kilometres. Its last launch was at Esrange in Sweden on 19 September 1983, and it left Libya in 1987. None of its recorded flights reached orbit. A second comparison is Interorbital Systems, an American company whose founders visited Tonga in December 2001 looking for a private spaceport, although Tonga has joined the Outer Space Treaty and the company remained under US law. Sea Launch, with its rig on Liberia's register, used a non-party only as a flag.

The potential is modest. A non-party host can lawfully say that it has no treaty duty to register anything, and can give a group something close to a home government that asks few questions. The strongest version pairs a stable host with founders who are not nationals of any strict licensing state, and buys only uncontrolled parts. It would still give no sovereignty, because the host is the state responsible in fact, and a host in that position can change its mind or be pressured to. North Korea, a heavily sanctioned state, has joined all four treaties.

odds.why: Small rockets from a weak or friendly host are possible, as OTRAG's tests in Africa show, but no such private venture has reached orbit. Treaty duties fall away for the host only, and customary law may still apply. Founders from strict licensing countries stay caught by their home laws. Hold depends on one government's willingness to resist pressure.

zones.name: Launching from land no state claims
zones.essay:
A very few pieces of land have no state claiming them. Bir Tawil, on the border of Egypt and Sudan, is the usual example, and Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica is another. A project might build a launch site there and argue that no country's "territory" is involved. It combines claims to unclaimed land with launching to orbit. The space treaties name a launching country partly by its territory, so land outside any territory looks at first like a gap.

The settled law starts with the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the main space treaty. A country is liable if it launches or procures a launch, or if the launch takes place from its "territory or facility" (Article VII). The Liability Convention and the Registration Convention define a "launching State" in the same words. Those tests are alternatives, so losing the territory test leaves the others. Nothing in these treaties says a launch must take place from a state's territory. Private people have no way to hold land as a state, because territory in international law belongs to states. The same goes for Antarctica under the Antarctic Treaty, which covers everything south of 60 degrees South and freezes the claims made by seven countries (Article IV). It reserves the continent for peaceful purposes, and its Article I forbids military measures, including weapons tests. It allows inspections by parties of all stations and installations (Article VII). The treaty binds its members, and the claim that actions by outsiders create no rights is an interpretation.

The open question is what unclaimed land does to the launching-state tests. Nobody has launched from such a place, so none of this has been tested. Reading the text, it seems that land with no sovereign gives no state "territory", so the territory test would simply find no one. That says nothing about what the launch is for the people who ran it, and it does nothing to remove the other two tests. A second open point is Antarctica itself. The Antarctic Treaty does not mention launches to orbit, and it would be for members to decide whether a launch from Marie Byrd Land fits.

Follow it through at Bir Tawil. The land itself is not claimed, and the reason is that Egypt and Sudan each prefer a different line on the border. Getting there requires crossing one of those two countries. A rocket, its fuel and a launch crew would have to come through their ports, roads and permits. Both have every practical power to stop such a shipment on their own soil and no duty to allow it. Rocket parts are also defence items under export rules, so suppliers need licences (22 CFR 127.1). If the rocket flew, it would climb over the desert and over its neighbours' airspace, which they hold under Article 1 of the Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying. Previous private claimants to Bir Tawil have not built anything lasting, and reaching it depends on the states next to it.

Marie Byrd Land is free of neighbours, and it brings another set of problems. It lies very far from any port. Fuel, food and shelter would have to come from outside, and even Chile's government settlement on an island near the mainland has a major hospital over 1,000 kilometres away. The Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the Antarctic Treaty that protects the environment, applies in unclaimed Antarctica as well, and a launch uses fuel and leaves debris. Treaty parties could inspect the site and could press the home countries of the workers. A US citizen launching there would need a licence just as anywhere else outside the United States (51 USC 50904), since the statute does not depend on who owns the ground.

Radio is the same as anywhere. A launch needs tracking and flight-safety links, and frequencies are coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union, whose members are countries. Without one, the launch cannot lawfully use frequencies and has no protection against interference. Damage is a harder matter. A rocket stage falling on a ship would lead the injured state to look for a responsible party. If none qualifies as a launching state, the injured party may be left with a claim in national courts against the individuals.

The potential is very small. Unclaimed land might in theory remove one word from the launching-state tests, and it does not provide access, supplies or protection. The nearest real cases are the Bir Tawil claimants and the Marie Byrd claimants, none of whom has built anything. Launch sites that have succeeded in remote places, like Baikonur in Kazakhstan, did so under leases from a state. The strongest version would be a small scientific rocket from Marie Byrd Land under a treaty party's national programme, which would add nothing to the argument for sovereignty, since that party would be responsible for it.

odds.why: Access runs through the neighbours or through Antarctic logistics run by treaty parties, so a launch site would be hard to supply. The treaties have other tests besides territory. No one has built anything at either place. A rocket from there would raise immediate concern, so holding it is unlikely.

zones.name: A leased launch site inside another country
zones.essay:
Here a foreign operator takes a long lease on land in a willing country and launches from it. This combines two zones that exist on land, leased spots and carved-out zones, with access to orbit. It is the strongest actual example of a launch site working as a place with special status. Baikonur, the largest and oldest, shows how far the idea goes.

Baikonur is in Kazakhstan and was built by the Soviet Union, with the test range founded in 1955. When the Soviet Union broke up in 1991 the site ended up in the new country of Kazakhstan, and Russia wanted to keep using it. Russia sought a 99-year lease, and it agreed instead to pay US$115 million a year for 20 years with an option to extend. The lease now runs to 2050, and all Russian crewed spaceflights leave from there. A second example is being built. Türkiye said in late December 2025 that it had started the first phase of a spaceport in Somalia, on land allocated under a bilateral agreement, chosen because a site near the equator gives rockets an extra push from the Earth's spin. Somalia has only signed the Outer Space Treaty without ratifying it, while Türkiye has joined all four main treaties. Italy's old launch platform off Malindi in Kenya is an older case of a foreign space programme working in another state's waters, and Italy has said it will reopen it.

The settled law is that sovereignty does not move with a lease. Kazakhstan remains the state whose territory Baikonur is in. Under the Outer Space Treaty, a country is liable if it launches or procures a launch, or if an object is launched from its "territory or facility" (Article VII). So a site like Baikonur gives at least two launching states for each launch, the operator and the host. The Liability Convention says the state whose territory is used counts as a participant in a joint launch, and launching states are liable jointly and severally, so an injured party can claim the whole sum from any of them (Article V). Armel Kerrest of the University of Western Brittany says states can share the cost by agreement, for example protecting the host when it takes no real part in the launch, but these agreements do not change the victim's rights. The lease operates between the two governments.

The open questions concern a private operator. All these examples involve states. Nobody knows how much a poor or weak host would be willing to hand a private company in a long lease, or whether a court would treat a clause giving a company wide powers over a leased launch site as lawful under the host's constitution. Honduras shows that such grants can be cut back when governments change, since it repealed its special-zone law in 2022 and its Supreme Court struck the laws down in 2024. It is also unanswered whether a host that is not a treaty party takes on duties merely by leasing to a party. Reading the text, it seems that Türkiye would be a launching state under the treaty for launches from Somalia because it launches. Somalia would not have treaty liability unless it joins the Liability Convention, though it could face claims in general international law. How the two states have divided this between them is not known.

Suppose a private company takes this path. It negotiates a 50-year lease with a government, and the agreement grants exclusive access, an internal security force and light taxation. The company is not a state, so it cannot register anything in its own name. Only launching states and qualifying international organisations keep registers under the Registration Convention. The host must therefore register, or the company's home country must. If the founders are American, they need a US licence for the launch wherever the site is (51 USC 50904), and British founders fall under the UK's Outer Space Act. If the rocket contains American technology, US export rules apply, and MirCorp, which leased the Russian station Mir, ran into delays in obtaining US export approval for a tether in 2000. The site needs frequencies through the host's membership in the International Telecommunication Union. Once anything goes wrong, the host faces the claim, so it will want a veto over launches. A change of government in the host country may reopen the deal.

Local people are part of the picture. Spent rocket stages from Baikonur fall on the ground along the flight path, and residents there salvage them. Scientific papers report harm to the environment and to people's health from the toxic fuel UDMH used in some Russian engines. A long lease gives an operator power over places whose residents did not agree to it, and that gives future governments a domestic reason to reconsider the terms.

The real potential is that this route exists and has run for decades, with the host earning rent and the operator getting access. Founders could use it to control launch access for a settlement. It gives real physical control over a site and strong practical autonomy. It does not give sovereignty, and the Baikonur rent shows what that control costs even for a major state.

odds.why: States have done this for decades, as Baikonur shows, and a private lessee is the untried part. The legal position is strong while the host is willing, because the host's law permits it. Rent and politics make it expensive. A change of government can reopen the deal, so holding for ten years is only moderately likely.

zones.name: Staying in orbit on no country's register
zones.essay:
Many people assume that a satellite left off the official lists is illegal, or that it floats free of all law. Neither is true, and the difference matters for anyone hoping that staying off a register could make a station independent. This entry looks at what happens when an object or station simply is not registered, whether the launch was licensed or not.

Registration means two things. The Registration Convention, a treaty of 1975 with 77 parties, says that when an object is launched into Earth orbit or beyond, the launching state shall enter it in a national registry and give details to the UN Secretary-General as soon as practicable (Articles II and IV). An older UN resolution of 1961 asks all states to supply such details voluntarily, so the UN keeps two lists. A launching state, under the same treaty, is one that launches or procures a launch, or whose territory or facility is used. The duty lies on that state. The Convention says nothing about private owners and provides no penalty.

The UN's own figures show that gaps are ordinary. In 2016 the head of the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs told the treaty committee that 92 percent of functional space objects had been registered across the two lists, and the same 92 percent figure appears in the office's presentation of November 2018, when 7,514 functional objects had been registered. Non-registration rose from 8 percent of functional objects launched in 2010 to 27 percent of those launched in 2014. The office listed the reasons, among them not being a party, launching states failing to agree on which of them should register, private activity without national regulation, and national mechanisms still unfinished. Crewed spacecraft and station modules are customarily registered, and all objects with nuclear power sources have been registered. No state lists all its non-functional objects. Later figures would differ, since launch numbers have grown.

So what the law settles is this. An unregistered object does not become ownerless or free. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty ties legal control to the state "on whose registry" an object is carried, so without a registry that article has no state to name. But Article VI still makes states answer for national activities, and Article VII still makes launching states liable, and neither depends on a register. Failing to register is a breach by a launching state that has joined the Convention, with no effect on what the object is. Resolution 62/101 of 2007 even contemplates the case, saying that if there is no state of registry, the appropriate state under Article VI can pass on information when supervision of an object changes.

The genuinely open point is jurisdiction. If a launching state has failed to register an object, the treaty does not plainly say who holds legal power over it and the people aboard. Kamil Muzyka, writing in Advanced Space Law in 2023, notes that Article VIII may be read as covering all objects, even those not registered, and he also describes registration as the administrative act that makes something a space object in law. Those two ideas pull in different directions. Reading the text, it seems that a launching state or a state with an Article VI duty could still assert authority over its own nationals on board, since nationality law works everywhere, and over the object as owner or licensor, but other states could question its exclusive control. A station has never tested this, because all crewed stations have been registered.

Suppose a group buys a launch from a licensed provider and asks that its station not be registered. The provider's country remains a launching state, and it has a duty if it has joined the Convention. Its regulators decide whether registering is required. The 2007 resolution asks states to encourage launch providers to tell owners to contact the proper states. Reading the text, a licensing state has little reason to agree to non-registration, because it stays liable anyway. If the group instead launches on its own from some place with no state support, it faces the problems of parts, port, insurance and radio that any such launch meets. In either case a station needs radio, and an orbital filing is made by a member of the International Telecommunication Union. A station with no filing has no recorded protection against interference, and other operators have no recorded obligation to coordinate with it. Nations track objects in orbit, so it cannot hide, and a large crewed station would be conspicuous to anyone with a radar.

People on board keep their nationality, so home-country laws still apply to them. Article V of the treaty and the Rescue Agreement oblige countries to help astronauts in distress, and they speak of returning them to the launching authority, which a group without a state lacks. A station on no register is also more exposed, and that is the real cost of the choice. Article VIII's rule that objects found elsewhere are to be returned to their state of registry protects a registered owner. An unregistered object has no state with a clear right to demand its return. A space lawyer, Michael Listner, has floated a rule under which an object with no registration and no apparent function would count as abandoned and free for removal, and that remains only a proposal.

The potential is therefore small. Non-registration gives no independence, and it weakens the protection the object would have had. The strongest version is an object registered late or registered by a state that keeps poor records. The nearest cases are the functional objects in the UN's count of unregistered satellites, and Swarm's SpaceBEEs, whose problem was radio licensing and not registration.

odds.why: Many small unregistered objects exist, so getting something up is plausible, while a crewed one is far harder. The launching state remains responsible whether or not it registers, so the legal gain is close to nothing. A missing register weakens the owner's protection. Nothing here leads to recognition.
