zones.name: A station registered with a small country that has no space law
zones.essay:
Ships can fly the flag of a small country with light rules, so people ask whether a station can do the same. A group would launch from some site, then have a tiny state enter the station on its register, and live under that state's nearly empty space law. This is a combination of orbit and the flag-of-convenience practice in shipping. Tonga's history with orbital slots makes it the obvious reference.

Start with what Tonga actually did. In 1987 a businessman named Matt Nilson, who had moved to Tonga, persuaded its king that even a tiny country could apply for positions in geostationary orbit, the ring above the equator where a satellite seems to hold one spot. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates radio use, accepts applications from member countries only. Tonga eventually held nine slots and leased them out, and a company called Tongasat ran the business. In 2018 Tonga's Lord Chief Justice ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. So the small state's right to apply was real, and it stayed the state's right, while disputes grew over who got the benefit. Later filings of a similar kind came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. In September 2021 Rwanda filed for two constellations totalling 327,320 satellites, which shows that a small state can still file for very large systems. Filing for frequencies is a separate act from registering an object, and neither of these cases registered a home.

Registration has a condition the shipping system lacks. Under Article II of the Registration Convention, only a launching state can register an object. A launching state is one that launches or procures the launch, or whose territory or facility is used. So a small country cannot accept any object offered to it. To qualify it would have to procure the launch, which it could do on paper by buying the launch itself or on the group's behalf. Tonga's position also shows a further difficulty. According to the UN's table of 1 January 2026, Tonga has joined the Outer Space Treaty and the Rescue Agreement but not the Liability Convention or the Registration Convention. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty speaks of a "State Party" on whose registry an object is carried. Reading the text, it seems that Tonga could fill that role under the treaty it has joined, with a registry it creates under its own law, and that small states that have joined nothing could not, since the article applies to State Parties.

What is open is whether a country that buys a launch only on paper really counts as procuring it. The treaty does not define "procures". It is also unanswered whether the state of registry must have a real connection to the object. Shipping law has a genuine link requirement (UNCLOS Article 91), although the same treaty does not say what happens if the link is missing, and space law has no such phrase at all. Adrian Taghdiri, writing in 2013, predicted that some countries would write loose rules to attract private space firms, and he warned of debris and of danger to passengers. A presentation to the UN's legal subcommittee in 2016 asked how the shipping concept would fit space objects. No court has ruled on any of this. Reading the text, it seems that a small state could lawfully be the state of registry if it has a real part in the launch, and that registration by a state with no part in it would be open to challenge by others.

What the registry changes is limited. The registering state holds jurisdiction and control over the object and everyone aboard. It is the law of that state that applies, so the founders move from one sovereign to another, and they gain only to the degree that the second one leaves them alone. Article VI still requires authorisation and continuing supervision by the appropriate state. If a small state does none of that, it breaches its treaty duty, and the state in which the founders actually live remains free to enforce its own laws against its own citizens. A US citizen on the project still needs a US licence to launch (51 USC 50904), and British founders are subject to the Outer Space Act. The launch site's own country remains a launching state and liable whichever register is chosen, and that country will impose its conditions first. So the launch provider's government decides whether the plan goes ahead at all.

The next steps are as follows. The group pays for a launch from a licensed provider, and the provider's state requires details of who will supervise the payload. A small state with no regulator offers little comfort to that licensing office, and it may refuse if the payload's oversight is unclear. Radio frequencies then need the small state's filing at the ITU, which it has the right to make. Banks would look at the small state's record. Insurers would want a clear legal system. If the station later injures someone or is in trouble, that small country has to answer, and a country with a tiny budget has good reason to set limits. Its law may also change with its politics, and the Tongasat litigation shows that local courts do hear such disputes.

The potential is real but limited. A small state's register gives a station a lawful home, with fewer rules and a more friendly regulator than a large power would provide. The strongest version is a treaty between the group and a small state that has joined the Outer Space Treaty, under which that state actually procures the launch, sets up a small agency and gets paid for it. That produces a privately run station under a friendly flag, with no independence. The state can still change the deal, and the station would have to live with that risk.

odds.why: Tonga and Rwanda show that small states can file with the ITU, and a small state could in principle procure a launch. A registry by a real launching state is lawful, which makes the legal odds moderate. The launch provider's own government can still refuse. The founders remain under a state, and that state can change its mind.

zones.name: A register run by a treaty organisation of small states
zones.essay:
The Registration Convention lets someone other than a single country keep a register. An international intergovernmental organisation, a body set up by treaty among governments, can take on the rights and duties of a launching state if it conducts space activities, declares that it accepts them, and has a majority of member states that have joined both that Convention and the Outer Space Treaty (Article VII). The Liability Convention has a similar clause (Article XXII). A project could try to use this route. A group of small states would create an organisation by treaty, and that organisation, rather than any one state, would register and supervise a shared station. This combines places run by international agreement with orbit.

The route exists in practice. The UN's table of 2016 shows objects registered by the European Space Agency (65) and EUMETSAT, the European weather satellite organisation (7), and the office notes declarations by others, including Intersputnik in 2018. So an organisation can register without being a state. It is also settled that the Outer Space Treaty applies to activities carried on through such organisations, and that practical questions are to be sorted out by its parties with the organisation (Article XIII). Liability does not vanish. Under Article XXII of the Liability Convention the organisation and its members that are parties are liable jointly and severally, with claims going first to the organisation and to the members if it has not paid within six months.

This is the most formally solid way of avoiding a single state's register, and it has limits that can be read from the text. The condition about a majority of member states means that most of the founders must have joined both treaties. UN figures of January 2026 give 77 members of the Registration Convention. Many small states have joined neither. UN officials have themselves listed organisations that fail this test among the reasons objects go unregistered. Reading the text, it seems that two or three states with the right memberships could form such a body, and that its status would rest on their real commitment. A treaty body made up of one small state and a private company would not qualify, since a company is not a state.

What is open is how slight such a body can be and still count. The Convention says the organisation must "conduct space activities", and it does not say how much. It also does not settle whether an organisation can be a launching state when it only pays for a launch from a member's territory, though the words "launches or procures" read naturally to include that. Nothing rules out a body set up for one project, and nothing has tested one. It is also unknown how a private company could sit inside such an organisation, since membership of a treaty body is for states, and how far the organisation could delegate its supervision to the company that runs the station. No such body is known to have been proposed, and no government is known to have addressed the idea.

Follow it step by step. Say three small countries sign a treaty creating an Orbital Authority, and it declares acceptance to the UN Secretary-General. The treaty can give the Authority legal personality under the law of its members, although other states need not treat it as anything more than their dealings with it require. It must then obtain a launch. The launch provider's state stays a launching state, keeps its own licence conditions, and will want assurance about supervision. Radio remains with the members, since filings with the International Telecommunication Union go through member countries. Founders who are US citizens still need a licence under 51 USC 50904, because the statute looks at citizenship, and a treaty among other states does not change that. Rocket and station parts remain under export controls, and export regulators will examine a new buyer of that kind.

Residents of the station would be governed by whatever the treaty says. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty speaks of a "State Party", and how this applies to an organisation is covered by Article XIII only in general terms. A treaty among states could make rules for criminal law, as the partners on the International Space Station did under their 1998 agreement, in which each partner keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens (Article 5), with special rules on crime (Article 22). A settlers' assembly might be given real powers by that treaty, and those powers would rest on the treaty, which the member states could change.

The route has some potential. It offers a station with several sponsoring governments, so that no single state's politics can end the project, along with a real legal personality and a right to register. It offers something closer to self-government than a private registration under one state. It also needs several governments to bear unlimited liability for damage on Earth, and most small governments would be slow to accept that for a private group's benefit. The strongest version adds a substantial state or a group of them with real space agencies. The nearest cases are the European Space Agency and the International Space Station, both built by states for state purposes.

odds.why: The legal form exists, and bodies such as ESA use it. Finding several governments to accept unlimited liability for a private project is the hard part, so the build chance is low. Once formed it would be legally solid, and that is why the law and hold figures are higher than for a single flag. Recognition stays low because the body is a tool of states.

zones.name: A private lease on a state-registered station
zones.essay:
Under this model a private group does not try to escape the state that registered a space station. It leases space or operating rights on the station and runs its own community there by contract. Residents sign a long agreement that sets the rules, the fees and how disputes are settled. This combines the idea of a lease with low Earth orbit. It is the form most likely to be built, because it asks no government to give anything up.

Two sources explain the idea. One is the ORBIS lease, a model contract drawn up by Spencer MacCallum, a scholar of privately run communities, and discussed by Alexander Salter of Texas Tech University in a 2019 article in the Journal of Air Law and Commerce. Salter starts from Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, which bars any country from taking space as territory, and argues that since states cannot extend territory there, rules for conduct must come from elsewhere, with a proprietary community as the best candidate. The other is MirCorp, which in 2000 obtained commercial rights to the Russian station Mir, with the Russian company RSC Energia as a major shareholder. It paid for the last crew to live on Mir, and it signed up a paying passenger before the money ran out and Russia brought the station down in March 2001. No settlement has used an ORBIS lease.

The settled law sits under any such contract. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty gives the state on whose registry an object is carried jurisdiction and control over the object and its personnel. Article VI makes states answer for national activities and requires authorisation and continuing supervision of private ones. A contract binds the people who sign it. It does not release any government from a treaty, and it does not take away any government's power. The International Space Station shows how registry law works in a shared habitat. Under the partners' 1998 agreement, each keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens (Article 5). The European Space Agency describes modules as treated like the partner's territory, so European law applies in the Columbus laboratory. Article 22 has special rules for crime, under which a country may prosecute its own citizens for what they do in any module.

What is open is how much room a state of registry may leave. Salter reads the ban on national territory as opening a space for private rule-making, and others reply that Article VI keeps private settlers under a country's supervision. Nobody has tested how much supervision counts as "continuing". A US licence requires insurance and permits the government to block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds, but US rules on occupant safety are largely on hold in a learning period set to end on 1 January 2028. It is also unanswered whether residents can validly sign away rights under the home law, or whether a private lease can have its own penalties. Reading the text, it seems that a contract can decide ordinary matters such as rent and house rules, and that serious crime and safety stay with a state. How a court on Earth would treat a contract clause that removes rights its own law protects has not been tested for a station.

Here is how it would go. A company registered in some state signs an agreement with the owner of a station, or builds its own under that state's licence. Vast's Haven-1 and the planned Axiom Station and Starlab are in this family, although none has flown or seeks self-government, and all depend on government customers or licences. The company writes a lease that sets a common code. A resident signs before launch. The resident's home state still reaches them as a citizen, including through tax in countries that tax citizens abroad. A resident who commits a crime on board comes under whichever state's law applies, and the company has no power to sentence anyone. When the resident leaves or falls ill, the return flight lands in some country, under its law. Children and inheritances would be handled by home countries, since the treaty does not mention them.

The practical pressure is on price. Launch alone, at about $3,246 per kilogram on a Falcon 9, comes to about $3.3 million per person each year just for food. Aurora Station offered 12-day stays at $9.5 million and closed. Bigelow Aerospace put $250 million of its founder's money into inflatable modules and laid off its 88 staff in March 2020. A lease does nothing to reduce that cost, and a lessee depends on the station owner for air and power, with limited ability to walk away. Export rules slowed MirCorp's tether, and the same rules would reach parts bought for a leased module.

The potential here is the largest of the orbital routes if the goal is a community with rules of its own and not a state. A friendly state of registry could leave most internal matters to the lease, in the way many countries let private housing associations or company towns run their own rules, and that could produce a real society with its own daily order. The strongest version adds a clause on arbitration with awards enforceable through courts on Earth, and an agreement with the state of registry about what it will and will not supervise. The limits are that the state remains free to change its mind, and that a resident can always appeal to it.

odds.why: Private stations are being built, and a lease among residents is a small legal step beyond that. The state of registry stays in control, so the law is usable only up to the limits it sets. Cost is very high, as MirCorp, Aurora and Bigelow show. It seeks no statehood and would receive none.

rules.says: No country may take space as territory, and Salter reads this as leaving room for private rules.

zones.name: Taking over a dead satellite or abandoned station
zones.essay:
At sea, an abandoned oil platform or an old fort can look like empty property, and the law of salvage gives people who rescue a ship in danger a right to reward. In 2016 the UN counted about 11,400 tracked non-functional objects in orbit, so people ask whether someone could dock with one, move in and treat it as found. This combines the idea of abandoned platforms with orbit. The short answer is that space law has no equivalent salvage rule.

Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, says that ownership of objects launched into space and of their component parts "is not affected by their presence in outer space". It says that such objects found beyond the limits of the state of registry are to be returned to that state. The Rescue Agreement adds that a recovered object is to be returned to the launching authority on request. Nothing in either treaty ends ownership because an object has stopped working. The Liability Convention counts component parts as part of the object. Michael Listner, a space lawyer, writes that there is no right of salvage comparable to maritime law, that a non-functioning satellite is not thereby abandoned, and that without the consent of the country that launched it the object cannot be disposed of or interfered with. Silent spacecraft such as Japan's SLIM lander and the Viking 1 lander on Mars still belong to their countries.

Some of this is less clear than it looks. The treaties do not use the word "debris" and do not define it. Nor do they say whether an owner can abandon an object. Listner reports suggestions that a state could expressly abandon an object by signing a waiver, or that an international body could declare debris abandoned, while noting that many states would object to the latter. He also floats a rule under which an object with no national registration and no apparent function would count as abandoned, and that rule is only a proposal. UN figures from 2016 show that no state reports all its non-functional objects, so many such objects have no register entry at all. Reading the text, it seems that an unregistered dead object still belongs to whoever launched it if that can be shown. If the owner cannot be identified, the treaties give no answer. A further open question is what happens when the state of registry has disappeared. Ownership of old Soviet spacecraft is treated as having passed to Russia as the continuing state, and the treaty itself does not address the point.

Consider what happens in practice. A group flies a robotic tug up to an old satellite without asking. The first problem is its own launch and licence. Its home state must authorise the mission under Article VI, and any responsible licensing office will ask about the target. Reading the text, docking with another country's satellite without consent looks like the kind of act Article IX of the treaty has in view when it requires consultation before harmful interference. A failed docking could produce a cloud of fragments, and the group's launching state would be liable for damage if at fault. Then the owner's state could object. Many satellites contain technology under export control, and Listner points out that handling a US object could raise those rules. The group would have no secure title, so no one could insure it or lend against it.

The lawful version already exists. Owners can consent. In November 1984 the US shuttle Discovery captured two satellites stranded in the wrong orbits, Palapa B2 and Westar 6, and brought them to Earth, and Westar 6 was later sold to the Hong Kong company AsiaSat. No dispute over title to those satellites is recorded, and the recovery appears to have served those with rights in them. Regulators have also shown an interest in satellites being moved at the end of their lives. In 2023 the US regulator fined Dish Network $150,000 for leaving a satellite too low. A market in consented removal would give a company legal contact with old hardware.

A dead object also has limited use as a home. Satellites are not built to be lived in. A retired crewed station is a different case, and those are rare and closely held. The Russian station Mir was brought down deliberately, and it remains possible that a government would prefer sale over disposal. The law would then treat that as a purchase with the state's consent.

So the potential is narrow. A group could seek express consent or a formal waiver for some old hardware, then reuse it as material. A state of registry could join in, and the combination would be lawful. Taking without asking is the version with no legal support, and its only real prospect is that the owner does not bother to respond. Even then, the object stays under the owner's law, so nothing about it would resemble a territory. The strongest version is a recovery agreed with the state of registry, under a licence from the group's own state, with the old hardware reused as raw material for a new registered station.

odds.why: Consented recovery has happened, but taking a dead object without consent has no legal basis, since Article VIII keeps ownership in place. Without clear title, money and insurance are hard to find. Owners and their states could object at any time. A salvaged object brings no recognition.

zones.name: People born in space and their nationality
zones.essay:
If a settlement lasts, children will be born there. The question is which country they belong to, if any, and whether a generation born off Earth could become the basis of a new nation. This combines long-stay orbital and planetary settlements with the law on nationality. No one has been born in space, so everything here rests on reading existing rules.

Every country decides who its nationals are. Two common rules exist. One gives nationality by birth on a country's soil, called jus soli. The other gives it through parents, called jus sanguinis. Most children born abroad get a nationality from their parents, although the details vary, and some countries limit how many generations can pass it on abroad.

Ships and aircraft have a special provision. The Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness of 1961 says in Article 3 that, for the purposes of its obligations, a birth on a ship or in an aircraft is deemed to have taken place in the territory of the state whose flag the ship flies or in which the aircraft is registered. Its Article 1 tells each party to give its nationality to a person born in its territory who would otherwise be stateless. This protects a child only if the child would otherwise have no nationality, and only among states that have joined. The treaty does not mention spacecraft. The Chicago Convention, on civil flying, gives aircraft a nationality and says nothing about a birth on board making a child a citizen. A US-flagged ship or aircraft outside the 12-nautical-mile limit does not count as US soil for citizenship, contrary to a common belief.

The Outer Space Treaty speaks of "personnel" in Article VIII, saying the state of registry keeps jurisdiction and control over the object and its personnel. The word suggests working crews, and the treaty does not mention birth. Whether a child born aboard counts as personnel is not settled. Article VIII cannot by itself give nationality in any case, since it deals with legal control and not citizenship. Reading the text, it seems that a child on a registered station would be under that state's legal control from birth, whether or not they were its citizen, in the way anyone on a ship is under its flag state's law. The reasoning for spacecraft under the 1961 Convention would have to be by analogy, and treaty text is usually read as written, so a space station may fall outside Article 3 unless its parties say otherwise. Nobody has ruled on that.

Follow what happens. A child is born to two parents on a private station registered by a European state. The parents go to their consulates, or send papers. If their country grants nationality by descent, the child has it with no great difficulty, subject to the ordinary paperwork, which assumes a registrar, a birth certificate and a named place of birth. No such place exists in the forms, and the station's state would need to set up a way to record the birth. Its law applies on board. A child with parents of two nationalities may inherit both. A child of stateless parents would be the hard case, with the state of registry as the natural candidate for a duty, if the 1961 Convention or human rights treaties were extended to it. Passports, school and medical records then follow the home country's rules. In a later generation, the descent chain may run out where a home state limits passing nationality to children born abroad.

Some of this feeds political claims. A people born in a place may one day say they form a people entitled to self-determination, a principle found in the UN Charter and in human rights treaties. A first generation of station children would not fit the usual meaning of a people under a colonial power. Over several generations the argument would become more serious. No court has considered it, and it may take a long time to matter. The Canadian Supreme Court's 1998 opinion on Quebec limited any right of breaking away to narrow situations such as colonial rule or foreign occupation, which is the frame such a claim would have to meet.

Health and ethics would come first in practice. The medical risks of pregnancy in weightlessness and under space radiation are not known, and no regulator has set rules. A US licence requires that occupants be told the vehicle is uncertified, and that assumes informed adults. A child cannot consent to living in space, and returning to Earth may become physically difficult. A settler's home country would have a clear basis for child protection law over its own nationals, and reading the text, it could press the state of registry to act.

The potential is that births give a settlement a real permanent population, which is one of the four tests of statehood under the Montevideo Convention of 1933. The strongest position would be a state of registry that passes a short law saying that a birth on its registered object counts as a birth in its territory, as some countries did for aircraft before 1961, such as Britain in its 1948 nationality law. That would solve the immediate problem and tie the child more closely to that state.

odds.why: No birth has happened in space, and it would need a long-stay station and a willingness to take the medical risk. Nationality law handles most such children through their parents, so the legal position is workable. A state of registry could easily add a rule. It would strengthen a settlement's population, but no state would recognise one on that basis.

zones.name: A habitat built in space from local material, never launched from Earth
zones.essay:
Imagine machines mining rock on the Moon or an asteroid and building a large habitat from that material, in orbit or on the surface. The structure itself never left Earth. The space treaties were written around things that are launched, so a home made entirely in space raises a real question about whether those rules reach it. This combines resources from bodies in space with a space habitat.

The words at issue are these. The Registration Convention applies "when a space object is launched into earth orbit or beyond", and it defines a launching state by reference to launching. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, gives jurisdiction and control to the state on whose registry "an object launched into outer space" is carried. It goes on to say that ownership of objects launched, "including objects landed or constructed on a celestial body", is unaffected by their presence there. The Liability Convention says a space object includes its component parts and its launch vehicle, and it does not otherwise define the term. So the text speaks of launching throughout, with one clause mentioning construction on a body.

Some things are clear even so. Article II of the treaty still applies, and no country may take a body in space by claim, use, occupation or other means. Article VI applies to activities and not to objects, so whatever people do in space remains a national activity for which a state answers, with authorisation and continuing supervision. That has nothing to do with whether the item was launched. Article I keeps space free for use by all. The machines that did the building were launched, and they stay under a state of registry. The people came from Earth and hold nationalities.

The open part is the status of the thing built. A paper in the Pretoria Student Law Review of 2021 asks directly how far the definition limited to "objects launched into earth's orbit or beyond" can take in objects constructed in space. It says there is currently no system regulating the status of objects built wholly or partly from lunar resources. Kamil Muzyka, writing in Advanced Space Law in 2023, describes "space-made products" as having similar legal recognition to classical space objects, and he says artificial structures made on other bodies might be treated as space objects if national law allows their registration, with the registering act creating the status. The words of the treaty can also be read more narrowly, and no general agreement exists. No court or government has addressed a real case. There is also the unsettled question whether taking local material counts as appropriation, on which states divide. The United States and others say that extraction is not claiming, and critics disagree.

Reading the text, it seems that three positions are possible. One is that a home built in space by a registered machine is a component of or product of that machine, and it comes under the same state. Another is that the structure is outside the Registration Convention, so nobody has a treaty duty to register it, though a state might choose to do so. The third is that the absence of a state of registry leaves it with no state holding jurisdiction under Article VIII, which still leaves Article VI in place for the people responsible. In all three, the operators remain under a state. So the strongest legal effect of the gap is on registration and on who holds jurisdiction, and it does not remove state responsibility.

Consider a real sequence. A company launches its builders under a US licence, or under another country's. That country is the launching state of those machines, and it must supervise the mission's activities. Radio links and tracking are filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. The machines work for decades and produce a large shell. Crew arrive on licensed vehicles, each with its own state of registry. A dispute or crime aboard then raises a question that has an answer in nationality, since every person there has a home state with some power over them, and a less clear answer as to the structure. Suppose the group tells its home state it is ending its licence and declaring independence. That state remains responsible for the activity under Article VI as long as those people are its nationals, in the usual reading, and it could prosecute any of them who return. Banks, insurers and suppliers on Earth would remain under its reach. The structure does not need supplies of building material, which is its real advantage. It would still rely on Earth for medicine, parts and new people for a long time.

A second problem is physical. Nothing like this exists, and no machine has built a pressure-tight shell from raw rock in space. Asteroid mining companies have run out of money. The Stanford torus and Kalpana One are design studies, and neither was funded.

The potential is that this is one of the few situations where the words of the treaties actually differ from the facts. A habitat from local material may carry a weaker tie to a launching state than anything built on Earth. A state could fill the gap by registering it as a matter of its own law, as Muzyka suggests. The strongest version is a settlement whose people have children, whose structure was built on site, and which has spent decades with light supervision. It would have a stronger argument than an ordinary station for being more than an extension of its founders' state, while Article II would still bar any claim to the body on which it stood.

odds.why: Nothing like this exists, and the technology is far from ready. The wording of the treaties leaves a real gap about objects that were never launched, so the legal odds are a little higher than for a launched station. Article VI still applies to the people and their activities. Distance helps hold, and recognition remains very unlikely.

zones.name: Capturing an asteroid and living inside it
zones.essay:
This idea takes a small asteroid, moves it to a useful orbit near Earth or the Moon, and hollows it out as a home with thick walls against radiation. It combines the law on asteroids with the law on stations. It also raises a question that the treaties were never written to answer, which is whether a rock moved by people is still a celestial body or has become an object.

NASA studied the first half. Its Asteroid Redirect Mission, proposed in 2013, would have sent a robot to take a boulder of about 4 metres from a larger near-Earth asteroid and bring it to a stable orbit around the Moon, for later visits by astronauts. An earlier study at the Keck Institute had looked at moving a whole small asteroid. The 2018 budget proposal called for its end, and NASA announced the close-out on 13 June 2017. Nobody has moved an asteroid, and no published plan for living in one is known.

The law gives clear answers up to a point. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, says outer space, "including the moon and other celestial bodies", cannot be appropriated by claim, use, occupation or any other means. An asteroid is a natural body orbiting the Sun, and it counts. Article VI requires authorisation and continuing supervision of private activity, and the US has a statute under which a citizen commercially recovering an "asteroid resource" is entitled to possess and sell it, while the statute itself disclaims sovereignty over any celestial body (51 USC 51303). The US State Department told Gregory Nemitz, who claimed the asteroid Eros in 2000, that private ownership of an asteroid is precluded by Article II. His case was dismissed without a ruling that decided the wider question. Laws in Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates and Japan follow the American approach of ownership in what is extracted.

The genuinely open point is size. The treaties do not define a celestial body and do not say how big a resource can be. A kilogram of water from an asteroid is plainly a resource under the US law. The whole body might be called a resource if it were small enough to carry off, and there is no agreed line. Reading the text, it seems that a boulder of 4 metres carried away would be treated as extracted material, whereas a kilometre-wide asteroid would remain a celestial body, even if it was moved. Between those lies a range where nobody can say. Another open question is what a moved rock becomes. It is not launched, so it does not fit the words of the Registration Convention, though the machinery attached to it does. It could be argued that the moved body is a space object owned by the mover, and it could equally be argued that any such claim is appropriation by use. No court has dealt with either view, and no government is known to have taken a position on this scenario.

There are also safety rules with real force. Moving a body changes its orbit, so the state responsible has a duty of due regard and of consultation before harmful interference (Article IX), and the Liability Convention applies to damage. Reading that Convention, it seems doubtful that an asteroid itself is a space object at all, since it is neither launched nor made. If it were to strike Earth, the victims would still have Article VI and the general law of state responsibility to look to, and any state whose people moved it would be the obvious respondent. Planetary defence was part of NASA's own study, so governments already link moving an asteroid with public safety.

A project would meet the following in order. It would need a launch licence for the capture craft, from the country of the founders. US citizens need one for launches anywhere under 51 USC 50904. Radio and tracking filings go through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. Any plan to alter an asteroid's orbit would be assessed by the licensing state, and it may well refuse, because the risk it would be accepting has no upper limit. Later, the people who move in would come on licensed vehicles under a state's register. Inside the rock, the law on board would be the law of whichever state holds jurisdiction over the modules and of the home countries of the residents. A company's claim to own the rock would be one more contested paper, since a state licensing the project has to take care not to claim territory by proxy. Article XII also opens stations on celestial bodies to visits by other parties' representatives, with notice, on a basis of reciprocity, which may apply to this one.

The practical side is also severe. Asteroids have very weak gravity, and whether a particular rock could hold air is not known. The two mining companies set up in this field, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, ran out of money and were sold in 2018 and 2019.

The potential is that this is one of the few settings in which the words "celestial body" could be tested, and a small moved rock might be argued to be property. The strongest version would use a very small body, with the state of registry for the machinery treating the rock as extracted material, and with international consultation in advance. That gives thick walls and a good legal argument about the material. It gives no sovereignty, and the legal argument would still be untested.

odds.why: No one has moved an asteroid, and NASA cancelled its one mission. The law lets a company own extracted material in some states, though the line between material and body is undefined. A moved rock would alarm governments, which could stop the licence long before it arrived. Distance helps once it is done, and recognition stays very low.

zones.name: A craft flying just below 100 km
zones.essay:
No treaty says where the air ends and space begins. A craft flying between roughly 80 and 100 kilometres up, or skimming the lowest edge of orbit, sits in the band where aviation law and space law are both arguable. Someone might try to use that doubt by flying where neither regulator can clearly claim the craft. This combines near space, the high seas and orbit.

The basic framework is settled, and the height of the boundary is what is missing. The Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, gives each country full authority over the air above its territory, and it states no height limit (Article 1). The Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, makes space free to all and bars national appropriation (Articles I and II), and it does not say where space starts. The UN's space committee has discussed the line since 1967 without agreement, and some countries oppose defining one at all. Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan use 100 km in their national space laws. The US armed forces call anyone who has flown above 50 miles, about 80 km, an astronaut. The astronomer Jonathan McDowell argued in 2018 for 80 km as better suited to the physics and to orbits actually flown. Legal writers also describe a functional view, under which a craft on its way to orbit counts as a spacecraft wherever it happens to be, and no treaty has adopted it.

What matters more is a point often missed. The line only matters over a country. Over the high seas, the open ocean beyond national zones, there is no national airspace at any height. UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, gives every country the freedom to fly over the high seas (Article 87). Space is free as well. So a craft over the open ocean at 90 km is outside national territory on any view, and the doubt about the boundary gives it nothing extra. The doubt changes which rulebook applies to the craft itself. If it counts as an aircraft, it needs a nationality through a register (Chicago Articles 17 to 20). If it counts as a launch vehicle, launching-state rules apply.

There is a real open point here, which comes from the Registration Convention. The duty to register applies when an object is launched "into earth orbit or beyond". A craft on an up-and-down path that never orbits seems to fall outside that text, a reading that fits the words but has not been tested. The Liability Convention has no such wording, but it also does not define a space object in terms of height. So a suborbital vehicle may be a space object for liability without being registrable. Reading the text, it seems that such a craft could end up on no space register, and if it also avoids an aircraft register, on no register of any kind. Whether a state can treat it as an aircraft is the next open question, and no court has addressed it.

Licensing does not have this gap. US law counts a suborbital trajectory as a launch, with a defined "suborbital rocket" (51 USC 50902), so a US citizen launching one outside the United States still needs a licence (51 USC 50904). The UK's Outer Space Act applies to its nationals for launching a space object. A state with national law on the subject can usually reach its own citizens without deciding where space begins.

Physics closes off the appealing part. The zone between 80 and 100 km is where air is too thin for a floating craft and too thick for a stable orbit. Balloons reach about 40 km. A satellite cannot orbit for long through that much air. A craft can pass through this band for minutes, as space tourist rockets do, or for a short period under continuous thrust, and nobody can stay there. So there cannot be a home in the gap, and a founder is always on one side or the other. Aircraft and balloons below about 50 km are in airspace on any proposed line. Satellites are above it. The Chinese balloon that US fighters shot down off South Carolina on 4 February 2023 was at about 20 km, well below all of this, and an analysis from Leiden Law School treated it as an aircraft in national airspace.

Other government controls also work. Fuel and supplies come from a port or airfield. Frequencies are filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. Parts count as defence items under export rules. Anything crossing a national border on the way up is in that country's air under Article 1 of the Chicago Convention.

The potential is small and concerns short flights. A company running up-and-down flights over open ocean might choose among regulators, and a state's own citizens remain under its rules. There is some room for a state to develop this area, for example by registering suborbital craft voluntarily. Nothing about the height band offers a place to live. The strongest version is a licensed suborbital operator under a light-touch flag, which is a business, and no one has claimed independence for one.

odds.why: No one can stay in this band, because the air is too thin to float and too thick to orbit. Doubt about the boundary gives little in law, since national licensing laws reach citizens anyway. Over the high seas the height changes nothing about national authority. Short flights can be run under licence, but they found no country.

zones.name: A permanently airborne airship over the high seas, registered nowhere
zones.essay:
Over the high seas, the open ocean beyond national zones, no country holds authority over the air. Suppose an airship stayed up there for good, crossed no border, landed nowhere and appeared on no country's register. It would have no airport to answer to and, at first sight, no flag state. This combines living in the air with the freedom of the air over the open ocean.

The settled rules are these. UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, gives every country the freedom to fly over the high seas (Article 87). That is a freedom of states, and a person enjoys it through an aircraft belonging to one. Under the Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, an aircraft has the nationality of the country where it is registered, may be on one register only and must carry that country's marks if it flies internationally (Articles 17 to 20). Article 12 says the rules over the high seas are those established under the Convention, and each party must make sure aircraft carrying its marks obey them. Article 5 gives flight rights over members' territory to aircraft of member countries, so an aircraft with no nationality has no right to enter anyone's air. Article 8 requires special authorisation for pilotless aircraft over a member's territory and tells members to keep such flights from endangering civil aircraft. The Tokyo Convention of 1963 gives power over offences on board to the state of registration.

No treaty clearly says that an unregistered airship over the high seas is unlawful in itself. The Chicago Convention places duties on states and speaks of aircraft that have nationality. It has no article on an aircraft without one. Compare the sea, where UNCLOS is explicit. A warship may board a ship "without nationality" on the high seas (Article 110). The same article applies "mutatis mutandis to military aircraft", which means military aircraft may do the checking, and it speaks only of ships as the target. Reading the text, it seems that no treaty gives anyone an express right to intercept a stateless aircraft over the high seas, and that physical interception of an airship by force would have to be justified another way, for example as defence of civil traffic or of a state's own security. Piracy is the one clear exception, since UNCLOS Article 101 covers private aircraft. Article 3 bis of the Chicago Convention limits weapons against civil aircraft, and whether it protects a craft with no state is untested. All of this is open, because no such craft has existed.

The physical part comes before the legal part. A permanent airship needs helium or hydrogen, fuel or sunlight, and spare parts. Even Stratobus, a French uncrewed airship design for 20 kilometres up, was planned to spend a couple of days a year on the ground for maintenance. A large aircraft has never stayed up for years. The Airbus Zephyr, a solar drone, can stay up for 64 days and carries no people. A crew at low altitude could breathe but would need food and water, and those would arrive by another aircraft. That second aircraft has a register and leaves from an airport in some country. Its pilots hold licences. The airport's government can ask where the cargo is going. So each resupply flight is a route by which a state reaches the project. Sick residents would go down in some country's territory or on a ship, and rescue at sea puts them ashore under that country's law.

The first lift also has to happen somewhere. An airship with no marks has to rise from a country's soil, or from a ship. A country would need to agree, and if it agrees it would likely want registration, which ends the plan. From a ship, the ship's flag state is involved, and a ship without a flag may be boarded. Wind then enters the picture. Air currents move a craft, and an airship that drifts into a country's airspace is, with no nationality, an unlawful intruder there. On 4 February 2023 the United States shot down a Chinese balloon off South Carolina at about 20 kilometres, a craft with a known state behind it and a dispute about its purpose. Countries also claim air defence identification zones, stretches of sky beyond national airspace where they ask aircraft to report in. About 20 countries and regions have these, so large areas near coasts bring a craft to military attention.

Radio is the next step. An airship needs to talk to the ground and other traffic, and frequencies go through a member of the International Telecommunication Union. A craft without licences that interferes with air traffic communications would become a safety issue for others. People on board remain citizens of their home countries, and nationality law applies to them anywhere. The United States, for example, claims power over certain crimes by or against its nationals in "any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation" (18 USC 7(7)). Money, insurance and supply all pass through someone else's rules.

The potential is close to none as a home and limited as a demonstration. An uncrewed balloon on no register might drift for weeks over the Pacific and be left alone. A crewed one over remote ocean might last until its first resupply. The strongest version is a registered craft on a light-touch aviation register, which is lawful and within reach, and which then carries that state's law on board. The nearest cases are Sky Cruise, an animation, Stratobus and Loon, all of which went through states.

odds.why: Nothing like this has flown, and even Stratobus needs ground time each year. No aircraft register means no right to enter any country's air, so any resupply or emergency meets a state at once. The legal case rests on what treaties do not say and has no support. Recognition would be remote.

zones.name: Aircraft flying under an unrecognised state's register
zones.essay:
A self-declared state could set up its own aircraft register, paint its own marks on planes and fly them, including over the high seas. This combines the unrecognised state with the open sky. The aim would be to show one of the visible signs of a country, an airline, with a nationality the state itself created. Real experience with disputed territories shows how this works and what it runs into.

Aircraft nationality works through treaty. The Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, says aircraft have the nationality of the state in which they are registered (Article 17), and that registration in a "contracting State" follows that state's law (Article 19). Article 5 gives flight rights to aircraft of contracting states, and Article 6 says scheduled air services need the permission of the state concerned to enter its territory. Article 1 says each state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the air above its territory. All of this is settled, and all of it assumes a state that other states accept.

The clearest ruling is English. In 2010 the Court of Appeal decided R (Kibris Turk Hava Yollari) v Secretary of State for Transport. KTHY, which the court described as a Turkish airline, had flown between Britain and Turkey since 1999, and in 2006 it asked to fly directly to Ercan airport in Northern Cyprus, which only Turkey recognises. UN Security Council resolutions 541 and 550 had called on states not to recognise the northern state. The Republic of Cyprus, the recognised government, refused consent. The court held that the Republic has exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above the whole island, though it has no control in the north, and that Britain would breach the Convention if it granted the permit. It rejected arguments that the treaty is suspended where a government has lost control. The airline also relied on the Namibia principle from the International Court of Justice, under which non-recognition should not deprive a people of the advantages of international cooperation, and the court found it unnecessary to take that further once it had ruled on the Convention. The appeal was dismissed. The ruling binds English courts only. The Republic of Cyprus has declared the north's airports closed, and trade goes through Turkey.

Open points remain. The judgment deals with flights into a recognised state's territory. It does not deal with a flight that stays over the high seas. Reading the text, it seems that an aircraft with a non-recognised register over open ocean breaks no rule about anyone's territory, since no country owns that air. Other countries would treat it as having no nationality under the treaty, because the state that issued the marks is not a contracting state. There is no general rule about what follows from that over the high seas, and no case has decided it. Whether an unrecognised state's register could count for anything in a third country that chooses to deal with it is a matter for that country. Turkey's position toward Northern Cyprus shows that a single sponsor can allow a route, and in that arrangement the sponsor state's law and permits do most of the work.

Suppose a new project does this. It sets up a civil aviation office and registers one aircraft. Pilots' licences come next. A pilot's licence has to be recognised to mean anything abroad, and the office will not be on the list of bodies other regulators trust. Next is the airport. Without a recognised state behind it, the project has no right to land in any treaty country, so it can fly only between its own strip and places that specifically agree. Aircraft leasing companies and insurers look at nationality and safety oversight, and the aircraft's manufacturer controls parts and technical support. Export rules apply to aircraft parts from many countries. Fuel on foreign ramps depends on a bank that can process the payment, and that depends on sanctions and on regulators. Radio use requires a licence through a member of the International Telecommunication Union, and a country outside the UN can join only with two-thirds of the members agreeing. Passengers carry passports, and a passport from a self-declared state has no code in border systems.

The result, in the cases that exist, is that an unrecognised state's flights run through a recognised patron. Northern Cyprus trade goes through Turkey. An unrecognised place with no patron and no land, such as a floating project, would have even less to work with, since it would also lack an airfield on land.

The potential is modest. A register and an airline carry some symbolic weight, and they can serve real people in a place with an actual population. They might feed into an argument about effective government, since international law takes some account of effective control, an argument the airline made and the English court did not accept as suspending the treaty. The strongest version has a patron state, an airline on the patron's register, and internal flights over the land the state actually holds. That is a working airline, and the nationality in law would be the patron's. Recognition has to be won through other channels.

odds.why: An unrecognised place could fly an aircraft, but treaty rights depend on being a contracting state. KTHY lost in the English courts even with Turkish backing. Parts, insurance and pilots' licences go through other governments. A few flights do not produce recognition, so that figure stays low.

zones.name: A high-altitude platform holding station over the open ocean
zones.essay:
High-altitude platforms are uncrewed balloons, airships or solar aircraft that stay about 20 kilometres up for weeks at a time, doing the job of a low satellite. Most plans place them over land, under the country below. A project might instead hold one over the high seas, the open ocean beyond national zones, serving ships, islands or a floating settlement, with no country below to ask. This combines near space with the air above the open ocean.

The settled rules divide cleanly. The Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, gives each country authority over the air above its territory, with no height limit stated (Article 1). Over the high seas, UNCLOS, the treaty on the law of the sea, gives all countries freedom to fly (Article 87), and the Chicago Convention says its own rules apply there (Article 12). An aircraft has the nationality of its register (Article 17). Pilotless aircraft must be flown so as to keep them from endangering civil aircraft in regions open to civil traffic (Article 8). Radio is governed separately. Paragraph 1.66A of the Radio Regulations defines a high-altitude platform station as a station on an object at 20 to 50 kilometres at a specified, nominal, fixed point relative to the Earth. The ITU Constitution treats frequencies as limited natural resources and forbids harmful interference (Articles 44 and 45). Filings go through member countries.

What is open is how the law treats these craft at all. A 2023 dissertation at the University of Pretoria describes a lack of clarity, because they sit between air law run by national aviation authorities and space law. At 20 km the balloon of 2023 was treated by the United States as being in its airspace, and an analysis at Leiden Law School agreed that a balloon counts as an aircraft under the Chicago Convention. Reading this, the better view seems to be that these craft are aircraft, though no treaty says so for this height range. A second open point is the coastal state's position over its exclusive economic zone. UNCLOS keeps freedom of overflight there as well (Article 58), so the coastal state gains no control of the air above that zone. Reading the text, it seems that a platform there is free to stay, though radio signals reaching a country's territory raise a separate question. Whether a coastal country must accept signals from such a platform is a matter for the Radio Regulations and that country's licensing law. Nothing has tested a long-term platform over the high seas.

Loon gives the most useful case. Google's balloon project started in 2011. It signed with Telkom Kenya in July 2018 and then waited until March 2020 for government approval, and because balloons drift, it also signed an airspace agreement with Uganda. It closed in 2021 for lack of a viable business. Stratobus, the French airship, has slipped year after year. These projects asked permission because their customers were on land, and customers are also what would bring this idea into contact with states.

Now the steps. The platform takes off from some country or a ship. That country registers it or requires a registration, and aviation regulators certify it. Stratobus's makers said flight tests had to come before certification and flight authorisation, for a craft with nobody aboard. It needs a frequency filing by an ITU member, which then answers for it. Customers on islands or ships pay through banks in ordinary countries. A ship receiving a signal is under its flag state's law, and a coastal receiver is under that country's. Winds can push a platform off its point, so a platform near a coast must be ready to enter national airspace or lose position. Airspace and traffic rules from the state of registry follow it, and an air defence zone may apply near some coasts.

Service to a floating settlement is the appealing combination. A platform and a sea platform would use each other, the sea platform as a landing or service place and the air platform as a communications link. Each would have its own flag state. That does not produce independence, and it adds more contact points with states.

The potential is real for commercial service and limited for territory. A registered uncrewed platform over open ocean, with one state's frequencies and licences, is likely to be lawful and probably workable, though no firm has shown that it pays. Crewed platforms are a different matter. Above the height where people can breathe the outside air, the craft needs a sealed cabin and carried supplies, and no such craft exists. The strongest version is an uncrewed communications platform for a sea settlement. It would serve the settlement well, and it would give it no extra legal standing, because the platform would remain an aircraft under the law of its register.

odds.why: Uncrewed platforms have flown under national permission, and flying one over the ocean is a modest step. The law is workable while the craft stays on a register and uses filed frequencies. Loon's closure shows the money is hard. A crewed version does not exist, and nothing here advances statehood.

zones.name: A Moon or Mars settlement by nationals of states outside the treaties
zones.essay:
Most space law binds a person through that person's country. So a project could recruit its founders from countries that have not joined the Outer Space Treaty, and have not signed the US-led Artemis Accords, then land on the Moon or Mars. The hope is that no supervising state, no treaty and no set of principles would apply. This combines the bodies themselves with the question of who is bound.

The membership facts are clear. As of 1 January 2026 the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, had 118 parties and 23 signatories that had not ratified. Countries such as Vanuatu, Palau, Kiribati, Nauru, the Marshall Islands and Liberia are outside it. The Artemis Accords, non-binding principles for civil activity on the Moon and beyond, had 78 signatories as of 28 October 2026. So many people have a home state outside both. Their home states have no treaty duty to supervise them under Article VI of the treaty. Treaties bind parties.

Nobody has tried this, and several parts are open. The first is customary law, the rules that bind countries because they are generally followed and accepted as law. Ram Jakhu and Steven Freeland examined in 2016 whether Articles I, II, VI and VII of the Outer Space Treaty reach states that never joined, in the context of mining. A piece in Völkerrechtsblog calls Article II customary, and it reports a broad academic view that the ban on sovereign claims also catches private bodies acting with state authority. A claim on the Moon by a non-party's government would therefore be widely contested, even though no court has ruled. The second is the position of people with no state behind them on the Moon. Reading the text, it seems that the treaty leaves such people with no state of registry and no supervisor, and it gives them no rights either. Article I gives freedom of use to "all States". Article IX's due regard rule protects States Parties. A private group with no state has no one to claim those rights on its behalf.

The largest problem is getting there. The Moon cannot be reached without a launch from Earth, and a launch brings in the rest of the law. Any launch site belongs to some country, and that country is a launching state under the Outer Space Treaty if it has joined, with a duty to supervise, and it will ask questions. Only a few countries have launch sites and rockets for this range. Every rocket that can reach the Moon has so far belonged to, or been licensed by, a member state of the treaty. Launching from a state outside the treaty has never been done for a lunar mission. The company that sold a ride would be under its own licence, so it would answer under its home law. A founder who has a nationality from an outside state could still buy passage, and the launching state would then register the craft and hold legal control under Article VIII, with the nationality of those aboard changing nothing.

Suppose the group manages all of this through a non-party host. It lands. Its radios need frequencies filed through a member of the International Telecommunication Union, and other operators then have no recorded duty to coordinate with an unfiled station. Its landing site may lie near an operating base, and the Accords' safety zones, or whatever rules the Chinese and Russian partners set at the International Lunar Research Station, may matter in practice even for those who never signed. Reading the text, signatories' zones do not bind outsiders, but those running them are not obliged to help an unannounced neighbour either. The treaties' rescue duties fall on states and flow toward launching authorities, which this group lacks. Supplies come from Earth, so suppliers are under their home export rules, and rocket parts from US makers need a licence. Its members have home countries that can stop their money, and a country outside the treaty can still pass a law against its citizens doing this if pressured.

The second reason for concern is damage. If a project without a state strikes a working spacecraft, the injured state has no treaty partner to claim against, unless the launching state is identifiable. That is why launching states and major powers can be expected to take an interest in any such project. China and the United States both aim for the area around Shackleton crater at the lunar south pole, so an uninvited group in that region would meet governments with strong reasons to act, though no treaty authorises anyone to remove it.

Nationals of signatory countries are also caught in a different way. The Accords are non-binding, and the Outer Space Treaty is what binds the signatories, so being outside the Accords alone changes little. A national of a treaty party who is merely outside the Accords stays under Article VI through the home state.

The potential is low. The real gain would be for a project with an outside state's government behind it, using that state's freedom from treaty duties and a launch it builds itself. The nearest examples are the ILRS partners, all working through states, and countries' own programmes. Outside the treaties a group gains a weak legal argument against supervision and loses the protection of Article VIII for what it builds. The strongest form would be a non-party state that sets up a real space agency, and that state might then choose to join the treaty for the rights it brings, as North Korea has.

odds.why: Reaching the Moon needs a rocket and a launch site, and nearly all of those belong to treaty members. Non-party status removes a treaty duty on that state only, and customary law may still reach it. Distance helps once there. Founders would lose the treaty rights that protect registered objects.

zones.name: A host state that withdraws from the Outer Space Treaty
zones.essay:
The Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, has an exit. Under Article XVI, any party may give written notice of withdrawal, which takes effect one year after it is received. So a founder might make a deal with a small state that it would leave the treaty, then host a settlement that claims land on the Moon or an asteroid in partnership with it. This combines a friendly host, or a state that could be bought or persuaded, with the bodies in space.

Part of that is simple. Article XVI is in the text, and any party may use it. No party is known to have used it. Saudi Arabia did leave a different treaty, the Moon Agreement, with effect from 5 January 2024, so leaving a space treaty is something a state can do and does. Withdrawal ends the treaty's duties for that state from then on. Under general treaty law, duties already incurred stay in place, and acts done before withdrawal are still judged under the treaty.

The open question is what is left after exit, and on this people disagree. Ram Jakhu and Steven Freeland discussed in 2016 whether Articles I, II, VI and VII apply to states that "are no longer parties", on the basis that some treaty rules have become custom, meaning they bind states regardless of treaty membership. A writer in Völkerrechtsblog calls Article II customary and cites Hobe and others as calling it a peremptory rule, one no state can opt out of. The same writer floats a half-serious experiment in which trends in US policy might one day erode the rule. A state that has consistently objected to a rule while it forms is sometimes treated as exempt, but a state that signed up in the first place would have difficulty showing that. Reading the text and these sources, it seems that a state leaving the treaty would escape its Article VI paperwork more easily than it would escape the ban on claiming territory, and an open claim to the Moon would be contested by most other states. Nobody knows how a court would decide, since no court has heard such a case.

Other treaties remain. Withdrawal from the Outer Space Treaty leaves the state in the Liability Convention and the Registration Convention if it has joined them, each with its own terms. Its membership of the International Telecommunication Union remains, so it can still file frequencies, and that is an advantage of working with a real state. A state with no space law also has few of its own restrictions, since the new law would be whatever it passes.

Follow the deal. A small government is approached, in the way that Tonga once leased out its orbital slots. Its people have to accept the arrangement, and the country's courts, opposition and media may not. In Tonga, a court ruled in 2018 that Tongasat had unlawfully received over $46 million in public funds, so such deals get reviewed. The notice is filed with the depositaries, the United Kingdom, the United States and Russia. All three would receive it directly, and a year must then pass. Aid donors, trade partners and major space powers will ask questions, and any of them could offer a reason to reverse course. If the plan is to claim land, those three governments have a shared reason for objecting.

Once the state is out, it remains a state, so it can recognise a settlement or claim land for itself. No other state has to accept that. Article II still binds all the remaining parties, so reading the text, they could not recognise national territory on a body without breaching their own duties. Rockets are the next problem. Any launch comes from a treaty party or the host itself. A treaty-party launcher's government is a launching state with duties to others, including the ban on appropriation, and it may refuse to carry a mission whose declared purpose would conflict with its duties. US citizens among the founders need a US licence wherever they launch from (51 USC 50904), and the US Moon Express letters of 2016 show how American officials link payload approval to treaty duties. Export rules apply to parts. So a host's exit does not reach the licensing laws of anybody else's nationals.

There would be costs inside the country too. A small state's only space asset may be its orbital slots, its registry or its voice in the UN, and leaving a widely held treaty could damage all of them. A US or European partner might also suspend cooperation with that country. Why no party has left is not recorded, and it may simply be that none has needed to.

Some potential exists. It is the only route where a real state, with real recognition, claims for itself something the treaty forbids its members to claim. That is why the recognition chance is a little higher than for other space routes, since at least one UN member would hold the view that the settlement has legal standing. The strongest version has a substantial mid-sized state and not a very small one, with its own launch capability. The result would be a national claim with few supporters, and it would not be a new independent country. Founders would have swapped private status for dependence on that single government.

odds.why: No party has left the treaty, and a small state would pay a heavy political price for doing so. Customary law may keep the key rules in place after exit, and other states' launchers remain bound. A real host does give recognition of a kind, which is why that figure is a little higher. Reaching the Moon is still the main barrier.

zones.name: Using safety zones as possession in practice
zones.essay:
Nobody may own the Moon, yet a base with a large safety area around it might keep other people away in practice. A group could try to build this up over decades, with one announced work zone after another, until it held a stretch of ground in all but name. This combines the settlement of a body with a set of principles written for avoiding collisions. It is one of the most discussed grey zones in space law.

The texts first. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, bars appropriation of the Moon and other bodies by claim, use, occupation or any other means. Article I keeps them free for use by all states, with free access to all areas. Article IX tells states to have due regard for the interests of others and to consult before activities that would cause harmful interference. Article XII says stations on the Moon are open to representatives of other parties, with reasonable advance notice and on a reciprocal basis. Those articles bind parties. The Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles with 78 signatories as of 28 October 2026, add safety zones in Section 11. A zone is the area where operations or an unusual event could reasonably cause harmful interference. Its size should reflect the operation and be set by commonly accepted scientific and engineering principles. It is to be temporary, ending when the relevant operation ceases, and signatories should notify each other and the UN Secretary-General. They commit to respect reasonable zones and to coordinate before operating inside them. Section 11 also says they will respect free access to all areas under Article I. The Accords describe this as a way of implementing the treaty.

What is open is how far this can go. No zone has been tested, and no court has been asked. The Accords depend on the word "reasonable" and on self-assessment by the operating state. Critics fear that a zone others must keep clear of could work in practice as a claim, since a site such as a sunlit peak near an ice deposit on the lunar south pole may be the only one of its kind. Supporters, including NASA, say that it respects the treaty, since it only requires notice and coordination. Only signatories have made that commitment. China and Russia lead a separate plan, the International Lunar Research Station, and have not signed. Reading the text, it seems that a non-signatory has no duty to respect a zone under the Accords, and that it does owe due regard under Article IX if it is a party to the treaty. Those two standards may not give the same answer on a real site.

International law on territory adds a further open point. A writer in Völkerrechtsblog notes that courts in territorial disputes have looked for what are called effectivités, acts of real administration such as making rules and running local government, and they have sometimes treated these as strong evidence of title when no one else has a claim. Under the treaty, such acts cannot produce title on the Moon. That writer's concern is that repeated acts of control may be used later, if the rule itself weakens. So safety zones matter as much for what they could be used to say later as for what they say today.

Here is how the process could run. A company under a state's licence builds a base near an ice deposit. Its state announces a zone of a few kilometres while vehicles land and dig. The zone is real and reasonable, because rocket landings throw dust at speed. As the operation grows, the zone grows, and because the base is permanent, the operation does not end. Other missions consult, and coordination takes time and data. A rival's request to work inside is delayed for safety reasons. The rule never says "no", and a late arrival moves elsewhere. Over decades, the base's neighbourhood looks much like private land. Residents make rules for the area, a security office directs visitors, and a registry records who has what. That would be a real practice, even if no one calls it property.

The limits are also real. A state makes the announcement, and a private group cannot make one alone. Licensing and supervision continue under Article VI. The state can change its policy, and other states can demand consultations. Article XII gives representatives of other parties a right to visit stations on a reciprocal basis, which is hard to square with a closed area. If an operator physically blocks another party's lawful mission, that party has a claim of breach against the licensing state, and it has no court with automatic jurisdiction. Harm would be handled by diplomacy, or under the Liability Convention's claims process. A small group could also find a bigger neighbour simply ignoring it. Moon Express's 2016 payload approval shows how US officials handled supervision case by case, with letters that do not bind a future agency.

The real potential is considerable compared with most space routes, and it would come under a state. A safety zone is probably the only lawful way to control access to a stretch of the Moon for a long period. The strongest version is a state-backed base with continuous activity, an honest engineering case for its zone, public notices and a record of allowing visits. That provides a working settlement with practical control over its neighbourhood. It gives no title and no independence, and critics would say it comes close to the line that Article II draws.

odds.why: A base on the Moon is possible within 25 years, though private ones are less likely. Safety zones are legal in concept and could be used to control a site in practice, but they rest on non-binding principles and one state's backing. No zone has been tested. Article II rules out any title that could support recognition.
