zones.name: A colony that declares independence after arrival
zones.essay:
Most routes to independence in space try to escape states before leaving Earth. This one accepts every licence and register on the way out, then declares independence once the settlers have arrived. It combines settling a distant body with the law on breaking away, and it has some of the historical logic of a colony that outgrows its parent. Since nobody lives off Earth permanently yet, all of it rests on reading rules made for other purposes.

Some things are clear. Issuing a declaration is not itself against international law. The International Court of Justice said so in 2010 about Kosovo, by 10 votes to 4. That opinion was narrow, and it does not mean that a declaration creates a state or that others must accept it. Self-determination, the right of a people to decide its political status, is recognised in the UN Charter and in later UN instruments, and it applies clearly to colonial peoples and those under foreign occupation. The Supreme Court of Canada's 1998 opinion on Quebec held that international law gives no general right to break away from a state that governs all its people without discrimination. The usual tests for statehood come from Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention of 1933, a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries.

Space law adds its own rules. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main space treaty, says the state of registry keeps jurisdiction and control over registered objects and any personnel in space or on a body. Article VI makes states answer for national activities. It does not end when a group of nationals stops listening. Neither article has any time limit or distance limit. Article II says bodies in space cannot be appropriated by claim of sovereignty, use, occupation or any other means. All this binds states.

The open part is large. The first question is whether a new state can come into being on a body where the treaty bars appropriation. The prohibition speaks of "national appropriation". A writer in Völkerrechtsblog, citing others, holds that it applies to anyone acting under state authority, and that exercising jurisdiction would count as a sovereign claim. Settlers who had broken away from their state would say they no longer act under it. Reading the text, it seems that the new body, not being a party, would not be bound by the treaty except through custom, while all parties would remain barred from treating any part of Mars as national territory, and that includes recognising it as such. Whether recognising a new state on Mars counts as appropriation by the recognising state has never been discussed by any court. A second question is the meaning of "defined territory". A settlement could say its buildings are the territory, since Article VIII protects ownership of objects, but objects are not territory. The third is whether settlers would be "a people" for self-determination. They would be a small voluntary group of various nationalities in the first generation. Children born there, and later generations, would have a far stronger claim on any reading. The Mars Society's writing assumes city-states will emerge with time, and how a settlement could move to self-rule under the treaty has not been settled.

Follow the events. A settlement of some thousands, under the register of one state, passes a resolution of independence. That state's first response is legal. It announces that its law still applies under Article VIII, and that it remains responsible under Article VI. It would be under pressure to show it is supervising, because the treaty requires it. It holds powerful tools, since supply ships, launch licences, spare parts, data links and the settlers' bank accounts all depend on Earth. A Mars transit window comes only every 26 months or so, so a cut-off would take effect slowly and be hard to reverse. Settlers' relatives and property stay on Earth, and the home state can act against them where they are in its reach, and against any settler who returns. The settlers' own treaties, passports and currency would have no standing without a recognising state. The rescue treaty speaks of returning astronauts to the launching authority, which then is the state they broke from.

Force is unlikely, and that is what makes this different from other routes. No navy reaches Mars in less than months. The home state might prefer to negotiate, and Canada's opinion about the duty to negotiate, though about a very different case, shows how law might respond to a clear vote. If a settlement can feed itself, the leverage falls year by year. Other states' interests also matter. A rival power could recognise it for its own reasons, as Russia did for Abkhazia and South Ossetia in 2008, which brought few followers and much dependence.

The potential here is the highest of any space route on the question of independence, while still very low in absolute terms, and it can only arrive late. The strongest version has a large, self-sufficient, multi-generation population, a negotiated transition with the state of registry, a new treaty among interested states revising Article VIII for this case, and a government that has been running its own affairs for decades. Nobody can say when this could happen, and it lies well beyond a 25-year horizon. The route also tends to work best when the parent is willing, in which case the outcome looks like ordinary decolonisation.

odds.why: Getting a self-sufficient settlement anywhere within 25 years is very unlikely. A declaration is not itself unlawful, but Article VIII keeps the state of registry in control and Article II complicates any claim to land. Distance makes it hard to reverse once done. Recognition within 25 years is unlikely, since the population would be small and the settlers still dependent on Earth.

rules.says: Issuing a declaration of independence does not itself break international law.
No general right to break away from a state that governs all its people without discrimination.

rules.says: No appropriation, states answer for national activities, and the state of registry retains control.
Tests for statehood include a defined territory and a permanent population.

cases.name: Sea Launch
cases.anchor: Launches took place on the equatorial Pacific, and the rockets were assembled at Long Beach, California.
cases.founder: Boeing with partners from Russia, Ukraine and Norway
cases.stopped_by: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2014, after a 2009 bankruptcy
cases.laws: Company registered in the Cayman Islands, vessels on the Liberian register, launches under national licences
cases.challenge: Boeing paid a $10 million penalty in 1998 over 207 export violations, and its licences were suspended for about two months
cases.recognition: A commercial launch business, with no claim to statehood
cases.cost: Boeing sued its partners in 2013 for more than $350 million after the 2009 bankruptcy
cases.story:
Sea Launch was a company founded in 1995 by four firms from Norway, Russia, Ukraine and the United States, with Boeing as manager. It launched satellites from the open ocean. Its rig, Odyssey, was a former floating oil-drilling platform that could move under its own power, and its ship, Sea Launch Commander, served as assembly plant and control centre. Rockets called Zenit-3SL were assembled in Long Beach, California, placed on the rig, and taken to the equatorial Pacific. Launching at the equator gives a rocket extra speed from the Earth's spin. By 2014 the company had launched thirty-two rockets successfully, with three failures and one partial failure.
The legal setup is why it matters. The company was registered in the Cayman Islands and its vessels were on Liberia's register, which the International Transport Workers' Federation criticised in 1997. Liberia has joined none of the four main space treaties. An article in the Journal of Legal Research says that launching from the high seas, from a platform registered in a non-party, by a private consortium, made it hard to say which state was the launching state, and that the problem reached the UN's space committee.
Governments reached the company anyway. Boeing paid $10 million in 1998 after US officials listed 207 export violations. US Customs tried to stop the rockets, classed as missiles, entering California. Pacific island countries raised concerns at the UN in 1999 about fuel from discarded boosters. The company filed for bankruptcy in 2009 and came out under majority Russian ownership in 2010. It stopped in 2014, S7 Group bought its assets in 2016, and the ships later moved to Russia. China has launched more than a dozen missions from ocean platforms since 2019, and a US start-up called the Spaceport Company has a ship of its own, so the method has continued.
cases.mechanism: A launch ship on a light flag lets an operator choose its launch site and avoid a host state. National licences and export rules still reach the company and its people.

cases.name: Boeing's 1998 export penalty over Sea Launch
cases.anchor: Long Beach, California, the home of the Sea Launch programme.
cases.founder: US State Department, Office of Defense Trade Controls
cases.cost: $10 million, of which $2.5 million was set aside for a compliance programme
cases.story:
Export controls are national rules on who may receive weapons-related goods and know-how. The United States runs its version through the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, usually called ITAR. The rules treat rocket technology as defence technology, so a US company sharing it with foreign partners needs a licence, and the technology has to be handled as the licence says. Moving a rocket project onto the ocean does not change that, because the rules follow the company and the goods.
Sea Launch tested this. Boeing managed the venture with partners in Russia, Ukraine and Norway. On 27 July 1998 the State Department suspended the project's export licences. Its Office of Defense Trade Controls found 207 violations between January 1994 and January 1998, in most cases because Boeing had not obtained prior approval of technology-transfer plans from the Defense Technology Security Administration. Each violation could have brought a $500,000 penalty, $103.5 million in all, and a three-year bar. A Georgetown University case study frames the choice officials faced as cooperation with former rivals against the risk of leaking missile technology.
Boeing agreed to a $10 million fine and a new document-control system, admitted no wrongdoing, and its licences were restored at the end of September. A criminal investigation was under way, and a Justice Department official said charges were unlikely because national security probably had not been breached. No part of the company's position on the ocean affected any of this. For a project that hopes to build in open water, the case shows that a government can halt a launch programme by suspending its licences.
cases.mechanism: Export rules follow the company and its technology, so a launch site on the ocean does not place a project outside them.

cases.name: Italian launch platform off Malindi
cases.anchor: Off the coast of Kenya, near Malindi.
cases.laws: A foreign space programme working from a platform in Kenyan coastal waters
cases.story:
The Luigi Broglio Malindi Space Center is a retrofitted oil rig off the coast of Kenya, run by Italy's space programme. It launched orbital missions from the 1960s to the 1980s, which makes it one of the earliest offshore launch sites and an early case of one country's space programme operating off another country's coast. A site close to the equator gives a rocket extra speed from the Earth's spin, and a platform at sea keeps launches away from towns.
Italy has announced that it will reopen the site after a gap of nearly 40 years. Kenya has joined the Outer Space Treaty and the Liability Convention, according to the UN's table of 1 January 2026, and it has not joined the Registration Convention or the Rescue Agreement. Italy launches and procures, so it counts as a launching state. Reading the text, a launch from Kenyan territory would also make Kenya a launching state under the treaty's words "territory or facility", and the two countries could agree how to divide any cost between them, as the UN recommended in 2004.
The platform shows what a real sea launch looks like when it runs by agreement between two governments. Founders hoping for a site with no state behind it can draw little from it, since every part of its operation has rested on one state's programme and another state's consent.
cases.mechanism: A foreign space programme can launch from a platform with the coastal state's agreement, and both states then carry launching-state exposure.

cases.name: OTRAG
cases.anchor: Stuttgart, where OTRAG was based. Test flights took place at Shaba North in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo and at Seba Oasis in Libya.
cases.story:
OTRAG was a West German company founded in 1974 by Lutz Kayser and based in Stuttgart. It is often described as the first commercial developer of space launch vehicles. Its idea was a rocket built from large numbers of identical mass-produced units, each made of tank tubes with a simple engine. Using kerosene and nitric acid and no pumps, it aimed for a launch cost about one tenth of conventional rockets, carrying satellites of one to ten tons or more.
It did its flight testing abroad. Its first flight was on 18 May 1977 at Shaba North, in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and it then flew from Seba Oasis in Libya. Its small four-unit rockets, 6 and 12 metres long, reached heights of 20 to 50 kilometres. Some had guidance or component failures. The company's last launch came on 19 September 1983 at Esrange in Sweden. It left Libya in 1987, and some of its equipment there was confiscated by the government. None of its 18 recorded launches reached orbit.
The case is the nearest example of a private rocket firm seeking room in a weak or distant host state. It shows how much such a firm then depends on one government. Moving test sites from one country to another was possible, and the firm kept its base in West Germany the whole time, within reach of its home regulators.
cases.mechanism: A private rocket firm can test in a host state with few rules, and it then depends on that one government and on its home country.

cases.name: Baikonur lease
cases.founder: Soviet Union, then Russia by lease from Kazakhstan
cases.laws: Inside Kazakhstan, operated by Russia under a lease running to 2050
cases.recognition: A treaty arrangement between two recognised states
cases.cost: US$115 million a year in the lease as first agreed
cases.story:
Baikonur is a launch site in Kazakhstan run by Russia. The Soviet Union founded it as a test range in 1955 for its first intercontinental missile, and it became the base of the Soviet space programme. All Russian crewed flights leave from there. In 1991 the Soviet Union broke up and the site found itself in the new state of Kazakhstan.
Russia wanted a 99-year lease. It agreed to pay US$115 million a year for 20 years with an option for a 10-year extension, and the lease now runs to 2050. Sovereignty stayed with Kazakhstan. Under Article VII of the Outer Space Treaty, a state whose territory is used for a launch is liable along with the one that launches, so each launch involves both countries, and agreements between them can divide the cost.
The site also shows who bears the local burden. Spent stages fall on the ground downrange, and local people salvage them. Researchers have reported harm to the environment and to health from UDMH, a highly toxic rocket fuel. Part of the site, Gagarin's Start, is planned to become a museum. A private group could hope to copy the form of this arrangement. It is the strongest example of a launch site leased across a border, and it rests on a superpower's earlier investment. No private lessee has obtained anything comparable.
cases.mechanism: A state can lease a launch site from another state for decades, with sovereignty unchanged and both states exposed to liability.

cases.name: Türkiye's spaceport in Somalia
cases.anchor: Somalia's coast. The exact site is not confirmed here.
cases.founder: Turkish Ministry of Industry and Technology and Turkish Space Agency
cases.laws: Land allocated to Türkiye under a bilateral agreement with Somalia
cases.story:
On 30 December 2025 the Turkish minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır confirmed that feasibility and design work had been completed for a spaceport in Somalia, and that first-phase construction had begun on land allocated to Türkiye under a bilateral cooperation agreement. The aim stated is independent access to orbit without relying on others for launches.
The reasons are geographic. Somalia is close to the equator, where the Earth's spin gives a rocket extra speed, and its coast allows launches over open water. Launches from Türkiye itself would have to pass over the Black Sea to the north or sensitive airspace near Cyprus and Israel to the south.
The legal position differs between the two countries. The UN's table of 1 January 2026 shows Türkiye as a member of all four main space treaties, plus the Moon Agreement. Somalia has signed the Outer Space Treaty and the Rescue Agreement without ratifying, and it is not in the Liability or Registration Conventions. So Türkiye would owe treaty duties as the launching state. Somalia has no treaty duty under those conventions, though the wording "territory" would catch it if it joined, and general international law may also apply. How the two governments have divided this between them is not known.
The project is also a useful guide to what a leased launch site requires. It rests on a government partner with its own space agency, and it follows a wider relationship between the two states. A private group would have neither.
cases.mechanism: A state with a space programme can obtain launch land from a state outside some of the treaties, and the treaty duties then fall unevenly between them.

cases.name: Rwanda's Cinnamon satellite filing
cases.anchor: Kigali. The filing concerns orbits and not any place on the ground.
cases.laws: A filing with the International Telecommunication Union
cases.story:
On 21 September 2021 Rwanda's government submitted a filing to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates radio use, for two satellite constellations named CINNAMON-217 and CINNAMON-937. The larger had 27 orbital shells with a total of 327,320 satellites, and the smaller was a subset with seven shells and 52,080. A filing is an early notice that a country plans to use certain frequencies and orbits. An earlier filing, ANTON-1N0, had been made on 20 August 2021 under the name of Marvel Space Communications Co, and it was not successful.
The Rwandan statement said such filings are essential to secure the possibility of future launches, and that it planned to become a hub for the African space industry. Rwanda launched its first satellite, RwaSat-1, in 2019 with help from Japan, and it passed a law creating a space agency in 2021. What Rwanda intended with the filing was unclear at the time, and it may have been linked to a private company or to its investment in OneWeb.
The case shows the reach of a small state's rights at the ITU, which treats every member alike, in the same way that Tonga's slot filings did from the 1980s. It also shows the limits. Rwanda has only signed the Outer Space Treaty and the Liability Convention, according to the UN's table of 1 January 2026, and it has not joined the Registration Convention. A filing does not put anything in orbit, does not register any object, and gives no one a place to live. Whether any of these satellites will ever fly is not known.
cases.mechanism: Any ITU member, however small, can file for very large satellite systems, and a filing gives frequency rights only.

cases.name: Interorbital Systems' Tonga spaceport plan
cases.anchor: 'Eua, one of the candidate sites in Tonga.
cases.cost: Seats were discussed at $2 million each
cases.story:
Interorbital Systems is an American company set up in 1996 by Randa and Roderick Milliron and based at Mojave, California. In December 2001 the two founders visited Tonga, a small kingdom in the South Pacific, as guests of Crown Prince Tupouto'a, looking for a site for a private spaceport. Matangi Tonga reported that 'Eua or one of the remote southern islands could become that site, for launching tourists into orbit at a low cost of $2 million per seat.
The attraction of a place like Tonga is clear. It is near the equator compared with the United States, far from cities and surrounded by sea, and its government had already shown interest in space through its business in satellite slots. The UN's table of 1 January 2026 shows Tonga as a party to the Outer Space Treaty and the Rescue Agreement, and not to the Liability or Registration Conventions.
No spaceport is known to have been built in Tonga, and the company has continued as a development-stage rocket business in Mojave, with its NEPTUNE, TRITON and TRITON HEAVY vehicles still in development as of October 2023. Its American founders and company would in any case have needed a US licence to launch outside the United States, whichever country they used, under 51 USC 50904. So the plan would have placed Tonga as a launching state by territory, and the US as one through its licensed citizens. That combination shows how little a small state can release a foreign company from its home country.
cases.mechanism: A US company looking for a launch site in a small state still needs a US licence, since the rule follows citizenship.

cases.name: Pegasus air launches
cases.anchor: Release points were over open ocean and varied by flight. Kwajalein was one of the support sites.
cases.founder: Orbital Sciences Corporation, later Northrop Grumman
cases.story:
Pegasus was a small rocket dropped from an aircraft. Orbital Sciences began developing it in 1987 with Hercules Aerospace and without government money for the development, and it has been described as the first privately developed orbital launch vehicle. The first flight, on 5 April 1990, used a NASA B-52. By 1994 the company had moved to Stargazer, a converted Lockheed L-1011 airliner formerly owned by Air Canada. The aircraft released the rocket at about 12,000 metres over open ocean, where it fell for five seconds before its first stage lit.
The aircraft took off from places including Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral in Florida, Vandenberg and Dryden in California, Wallops in Virginia, Kwajalein in the Pacific, and the Canary Islands in the Atlantic. There were 46 launches in all, with the last listed as 3 July 2026.
The rocket matters here because at the moment of release nothing is below it except open sea, and the launch site is an aircraft. The Outer Space Treaty speaks of a state's "territory or facility", and nobody has had to say whether a registered aircraft is a facility of the state of registry, or whether an airport used to take off counts as territory used for the launch. These questions did not come up because the company was American, its launches were licensed, and no damage claim is known. Pegasus shows that the technique works. It shows nothing about doing it without a state.
cases.mechanism: A rocket released from a registered aircraft over the sea needs no launch pad or host, and the aircraft and company stay under national law.

cases.name: KTHY and direct flights to Northern Cyprus
aka: R (Kibris Turk Hava Yollari) v Secretary of State for Transport
cases.anchor: Ercan airport in Northern Cyprus, the destination in dispute. The court sat in London.
cases.founder: Kibris Turk Hava Yollari and CTA Holidays
cases.recognition: Northern Cyprus is recognised only by Turkey
cases.story:
In November 2006 the airline Kibris Turk Hava Yollari, or KTHY, and a holiday company applied to Britain for permission to fly directly between the United Kingdom and Ercan airport in Northern Cyprus. The court described KTHY as a Turkish airline. It had flown between Britain and Turkey since 1999. Northern Cyprus declared independence in 1983, UN Security Council resolutions 541 and 550 called the declaration invalid and asked states not to recognise it, and only Turkey has done so.
Britain refused, and the companies sued. The High Court judge, Wyn Williams J, held that under the Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, the Republic of Cyprus has exclusive sovereignty over the air above the whole island, including the north where it has no control. Article 6 says scheduled flights into a state's territory need that state's permission, and Cyprus had refused. A permit from Britain would therefore breach the treaty.
On appeal in 2010 the companies argued that a treaty must be read realistically, and that rights over territory lapse when a government loses effective control. They pointed to the principle in the International Court of Justice's Namibia opinion, that non-recognition should not deprive people of the benefits of international cooperation. The Court of Appeal rejected the argument on the Convention and dismissed the appeal. It found no need to take the recognition point further.
The case is the leading illustration of how the air treaty treats a place without recognition. Practical control of an airport did not give access to the air routes of the world, and the recognised state's rights survived a long loss of control. The ruling binds English courts only.
cases.mechanism: Air treaty rights follow recognised sovereignty, so a recognised government can block flights to a place it does not control.

cases.name: UN resolutions on the launching state and on registration
cases.anchor: Vienna, home of the UN's space office.
cases.story:
The Liability Convention of 1972 and the Registration Convention of 1975 use the words "launching State" for a country that launches or procures a launch, or from whose territory or facility an object is launched. By the 1990s these words raised new problems. Private companies were buying launches across borders, and Sea Launch was firing rockets from a Liberian-registered rig on the open ocean. The UN's space committee took up a review of the concept.
The results were two General Assembly resolutions. Resolution 59/115, adopted on 10 December 2004, recommends that countries consider national laws to authorise and supervise non-governmental space activities, consider agreements on joint launches, and share their practice on transferring ownership of objects in orbit. It says plainly that nothing in it is an authoritative interpretation of, or a proposed amendment to, the two treaties.
Resolution 62/101, adopted in 2007, is about registration practice. It recommends that the state of the launch territory, where no prior agreement exists, contact those that could qualify as launching states so that they can jointly decide who registers, that launch providers advise owners to approach the proper states, and that after a change of supervision in orbit the state of registry report the new owner, orbit and function. It adds that if there is no state of registry, the appropriate state under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty could send in that information.
General Assembly resolutions of this type are recommendations. So the words "territory or facility" remain undefined, and nobody can use these texts to settle whether a flagged or unflagged platform is a facility. They do show that governments know of the gaps and chose to answer them with national laws and agreements, leaving the treaties unchanged.
cases.mechanism: The UN answered the gaps in the launching-state concept with recommendations, leaving the treaty wording as it was.

cases.name: Unregistered objects in UN figures
cases.anchor: Vienna, home of the UN's space office.
cases.founder: UN Office for Outer Space Affairs
cases.laws: Registration Convention and General Assembly resolution 1721B
cases.story:
The UN keeps a register of objects launched into space. Two sources feed it. A General Assembly resolution of 1961, 1721B, asks states to supply information voluntarily. The Registration Convention of 1975 requires launching states that have joined it to supply it.
In April 2016 the head of the UN's space office, Simonetta Di Pippo, gave the treaty committee the figures. As of 1 April 2016, 6,772 functional objects had been registered, and across the two lists 92 percent of functional objects had been registered since 1957. Among those in Earth orbit or beyond at that date, 89 percent were registered. Non-registration of functional objects rose from 8 percent of those launched in 2010 to 27 percent of those launched in 2014, and 72 percent of those launched in 2015 were still unregistered at that time, with the office expecting that to fall to 7 percent after states sent in their submissions. A UN presentation of November 2018 gave 7,514 registered functional objects, again with the 92 percent overall figure.
The office gave reasons. A state may not be a party. Several launching states may not have agreed who should register. Private firms may be operating without national regulation. National procedures may be incomplete. A launching state may not "claim" an object. An intergovernmental body may not meet the conditions to act as a launching state. No state of registry reports all its non-functional objects, and about 11,400 of the tracked objects were debris. Crewed spacecraft and space station elements are customarily registered.
The numbers show that an unregistered object is common and that nothing legal happens to it on that account. They do not show that any station or crewed craft has stayed off a register, since none is reported to have. These figures stop at 2018, and launch numbers have grown since.
cases.mechanism: Registration is a duty on launching states, and about one functional object in twelve had missed it by 2018, with no consequence for the object itself.

cases.name: Recovery of Palapa B2 and Westar 6
cases.anchor: Kennedy Space Center, where the shuttle flight began. The recovery took place in low Earth orbit.
cases.story:
Earlier in 1984 the Space Shuttle mission STS-41-B released two communications satellites, Palapa B2 and Westar 6. Their kick motors, which were meant to raise them to high orbit, malfunctioned and left them stranded in the wrong orbits. Ground controllers lowered them from about 970 kilometres to about 340 kilometres so that a shuttle could reach them.
In November 1984 the shuttle Discovery, on mission STS-51-A, met them. On the fifth day of the mission the astronauts Joseph Allen and Dale Gardner went outside, caught Palapa B2 with a device inserted in its motor nozzle, and brought it into the payload bay. They recovered Westar 6 the next day. Gardner held up a "For Sale" sign. Both came back to Earth, and Westar 6 was later sold to AsiaSat, a company based in Hong Kong.
This is the closest thing in space history to a salvage, and it appears to have worked because the people with rights in the satellites wanted them back. No dispute over title is recorded. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty says that ownership of a space object is not affected by its presence in space or by its return to Earth, and space lawyers say there is no right of salvage comparable to the one at sea. So the mission does not show that anyone may take a dead satellite. It shows that a dead satellite can be recovered and resold when the owner agrees, and that the hardware then has a new life on Earth under ordinary property law.
cases.mechanism: Recovering a stranded satellite is possible when the owner agrees. No treaty gives a stranger a right to do it.

cases.name: NASA Asteroid Redirect Mission
cases.anchor: NASA headquarters in Washington. The target was a near-Earth asteroid and then lunar orbit.
cases.story:
The Asteroid Redirect Mission was a NASA proposal of 2013. A robotic spacecraft would rendezvous with a large near-Earth asteroid, use grippers and a drill to take a boulder of about 4 metres, and carry it to a stable orbit around the Moon. Astronauts on an Orion capsule would later visit it, possibly in 2026, and the mission would also test ways of deflecting an asteroid to protect Earth. An earlier version looked at bringing back a whole small asteroid, and a feasibility study from the Keck Institute for Space Studies had looked at that in 2012.
If funded, it would have launched in December 2021. The proposed 2018 budget called for its cancellation, it received notice of defunding in April 2017, and NASA announced the close-out on 13 June 2017. Its ion thruster work continued.
The mission is the nearest thing to a plan to move part of a celestial body. It would have been a government project, under US jurisdiction, and the question of what a moved boulder is under space law never had to be answered. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty bars appropriation of celestial bodies by claim, use or occupation. Article VIII speaks of objects launched or constructed, and a boulder is neither. The US law of 2015 lets American citizens own asteroid resources they recover, without saying how large a resource can be. Nobody now knows whether a moved boulder would be treated as a resource, as a body or as a new object.
cases.mechanism: A government plan to bring a boulder to lunar orbit was cancelled before the legal status of a moved rock was ever tested.

cases.name: Article 3 of the 1961 Statelessness Convention
cases.anchor: New York, where the treaty was done.
cases.laws: Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness
cases.story:
A stateless person is someone no country treats as its national. In 1961 countries meeting in New York agreed the Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness to limit how often that happens, and it entered into force on 13 December 1975. Article 1 tells each party to grant its nationality to a person born in its territory who would otherwise be stateless.
The drafters saw that some births happen in no territory, so they wrote Article 3. For the purpose of the parties' duties under the treaty, birth on a ship or in an aircraft is deemed to have taken place in the territory of the state whose flag the ship flies or in which the aircraft is registered. Without this, a child born in mid-ocean to stateless parents could fall through the rule. The article has a narrow reach. It works only where the child would otherwise have no nationality, and among states that have joined. Most children get a nationality from their parents, so it rarely applies. A birth on a US-flagged ship or aircraft outside the 12-mile limit does not of itself make a child American.
Spacecraft are not mentioned. The Outer Space Treaty came six years later, and it speaks only of "personnel" on registered objects. A parent or lawyer might argue that a space station is similar enough that Article 3 should apply by analogy, or that a state of registry has the same duty. Nothing has tested that. A state of registry could remove the doubt by passing its own law, as Britain did for aircraft in its British Nationality Act 1948, section 32(5).
cases.mechanism: The treaty treats a birth on a ship or aircraft as a birth in the flag or registry state, and it does not mention spacecraft.

cases.name: Does the Outer Space Treaty bind non-parties
cases.anchor: Vienna, home of the UN's space office, which publishes the list of members.
cases.story:
A treaty binds the countries that join it. As of 1 January 2026 the Outer Space Treaty had 118 parties and 23 signatories that had not ratified. Dozens of countries are outside it. International law has a second source, custom, which is a rule that binds states because they generally follow it and treat it as law. A treaty rule can become custom, and it then binds countries that never joined.
Whether that has happened to the Outer Space Treaty, and to which articles, is a live question. In 2016 Ram Jakhu and Steven Freeland presented a paper at the International Astronautical Congress examining whether Articles I, II, VI and VII reach states that never joined or are no longer parties, in the setting of mining in space. A writer in Völkerrechtsblog calls Articles II and III customary, and cites Hobe and others as treating the ban on appropriation as a peremptory norm, a rule no state can opt out of. The same writer notes a half-serious argument that the rule might weaken if powerful states keep testing it. Writers on the Moon Agreement have also argued about custom, in the opposite direction, saying that silence from non-parties could have let its ideas become custom until a US executive order of 2020 expressly rejected them.
No court has ruled. The practical importance is that this is the point at which every plan to use a non-party host or a withdrawal from the treaty has to stop and ask whether the rule followed them out. The treaty's own Article XVI lets a party leave on one year's notice, and no party is known to have done so.
cases.mechanism: Treaty rules can become custom and so bind non-parties. Which articles of the Outer Space Treaty have done so has not been decided.
